problem-framing.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have "framed the problem" if your one-sentence problem already contains your product (e.g. "users need our AI dashboard"). problem-framing.text: A team spends four months and $200k building a beautifully engineered feature nobody opens — because on day one they wrote "users want a recommendations tab" instead of asking whose problem it solved, and whether that problem was even real. The frame is the cheapest thing you will ever build and the only one that decides whether the other four months are worth building at all.

Every product bet starts ambiguous: a hunch, a loud customer, a competitor's move, a roadmap deadline. The Problem Frame converts "we should build something" into one customer problem, one segment, one riskiest assumption, and the exact evidence that would invalidate it — Section 1 of the decision packet you carry through discovery, PRD, instrumentation, experiment, launch, and the feedback report.

problem-framing.prompt: "Users want a recommendations tab." Before you scope it — what is wrong with that as a problem statement? Answer before reading on.
problem-framing.reveal: It is a solution pretending to be a problem. "Recommendations tab" already presumes the problem is discovery, the cause is too many choices, and the fix is a tab — three unproven leaps, and it never says WHO. The real frame: "New shoppers in their first session abandon the catalog before finding a product they like; we believe most cannot narrow 4,000 items down fast enough." Naming the feature first feels like momentum while quietly deciding the answer and skipping customer discovery entirely.

problem-framing.code:
# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## 1. Frame
- Customer problem (one sentence, no product in it):
    New shoppers abandon the catalog in session 1 before finding a product they like
- Segment (who has it, specifically):
    First-time visitors, mobile, arriving from paid social (not returning power users)
- Riskiest assumption (write it so it can be proven FALSE):
    Most first-time mobile shoppers CANNOT narrow 4,000 items to a shortlist unaided
- Invalidation threshold (the number that kills the idea):
    < 6 of 12 discovery interviews describe "too many choices" unprompted  -> STOP
- Activation metric this idea would move:
    % of session-1 shoppers who view a product detail page within 90s

<!-- Sections 2-5 (discovery notes, experiment, metric tree, decision memo) added downstream. -->
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
The customer problem line: One sentence, no product in it. If it names a feature, a tab, or a technology, you smuggled in the answer and skipped discovery. Describe the pain, not the fix.

The segment: Whose problem, specifically. "Users" is not a segment. First-time vs returning, mobile vs desktop, paid vs organic — these change the whole bet, and a diffuse segment is a frame you cannot test.
The riskiest assumption: The single belief that, if false, makes the idea worthless. Write it so it can return "no". "Users will love it" cannot be falsified; "most cannot self-narrow" can.
The invalidation threshold: A number, decided BEFORE you gather evidence, that tells you to stop. Setting it after you see the data is how teams rationalize building the thing anyway.
The activation metric: Name the one behavioral metric this idea would move if the problem is real. It seeds the metric tree and the experiment — and stops you shipping something you cannot measure.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

problem-framing.starter:
# Writing Section 1 of the decision packet, one line at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real product idea you are tempted to build and write the Problem Frame: the customer's actual problem in one solution-free sentence, the market segment who has it, the assumption that — if false — kills the idea, and the invalidation threshold that would tell you to stop. No feature in the frame.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only abandonment_by_segment at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your one-sentence problem aloud. If it contains a feature name, a UI element, or a technology, you have a product in it — cut it until only the customer's pain remains.
# 2. Check the segment is specific enough to recruit for discovery: could you list five real people who fit it? "Users" fails; "first-time mobile shoppers from paid social" passes.
# 3. Confirm the riskiest assumption can return "no". Write the exact interview or data result that would falsify it. If nothing could, it is a wish, not an assumption.
# 4. Confirm the invalidation threshold is a NUMBER set before evidence (e.g. "<6 of 12 interviews"), not a feeling you will calibrate after seeing the data.
# 5. Name the one activation or retention metric this idea would move. If you cannot, you will not be able to design an experiment or read the feedback loop later.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

SESSIONS = [
    ("new-mobile", False), ("new-mobile", False), ("new-mobile", True),
    ("new-mobile", False), ("new-mobile", False), ("new-mobile", True),
    ("new-mobile", False), ("new-mobile", False), ("new-mobile", True),
    ("new-mobile", False),
    ("new-desktop", True), ("new-desktop", False), ("new-desktop", True),
    ("new-desktop", False), ("new-desktop", True), ("new-desktop", False),
    ("new-desktop", True), ("new-desktop", False), ("new-desktop", True),
    ("new-desktop", False),
    ("returning", True), ("returning", True), ("returning", False),
    ("returning", True), ("returning", True), ("returning", True),
    ("returning", False), ("returning", True), ("returning", True),
    ("returning", True),
]
KILL_LINE = 55.0


def abandonment_by_segment(sessions):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

rates = abandonment_by_segment(SESSIONS)
for seg in sorted(rates):
    a, t = rates[seg]
    print(f"segment {seg}: abandonment {a / t * 100:.1f}% ({a}/{t})")
worst = max(sorted(rates), key=lambda s: rates[s][0] / rates[s][1])
wa, wt = rates[worst]
worst_pct = wa / wt * 100
print(f"worst segment: {worst} at {worst_pct:.1f}%")
verdict = "FRAME HOLDS" if worst_pct >= KILL_LINE else "STOP - problem too small"
print(f"kill-line {KILL_LINE:.1f}%: {verdict}")

kill-line 55.0%: FRAME HOLDS

storyboard.say: Every product bet starts as a hunch. The Problem Frame is the cheapest thing you build to turn that hunch into a decision.
Start with the customer problem, stated in one product-free sentence. It defines what the bet is actually about.
Next, the market segment scopes exactly who has this problem, so the bet answers for a real population, not everyone.
Now name the one riskiest assumption that, if false, kills the whole idea outright.
An assumption alone is a wish. The invalidation threshold makes it falsifiable, with a number that decides it.
That threshold is the trigger: it either kills the bet or clears it. Discovery evidence hits this line first.
The product is deliberately out. It must not leak into the problem statement — it belongs to the PRD after the frame validates.
The invariant: the frame holds the customer's pain and the evidence that ends the bet, never your solution.

problem-framing.text: The tell that separates a senior PM from a feature-factory PM: they write the invalidation threshold BEFORE gathering evidence, and they honor it. If your "validation" plan has no number that could make you cancel the idea, you are not running discovery — you are collecting quotes to justify a build you already approved. (This is the evidence-based discipline behind NIST's MEASURE function (test, evaluation, verification, and validation) and ABET's evidence-based decision outcomes: a claim you cannot test is not evidence.) (Note: 'falsifiability' is not NIST RMF language; MEASURE frames this as TEVV / measurable evidence.)

problem-framing.question: Which of these is a real Problem Frame rather than a disguised solution?
options: "Our activation is low, so we should add an onboarding checklist."

"Let's build AI recommendations to increase engagement."

customer-discovery.outcome: Take one real product idea you are tempted to build and run customer discovery on it FIRST: turn a risky assumption into an interview + experiment, read the activation/retention signal, and write the decision packet that says build, pivot, or kill — with the invalidation threshold set BEFORE you look at the data.
customer-discovery.proof: customer_experiment_and_metric_decision_packet.md: the riskiest assumption named, 3+ discovery interview questions that can return a NO, an experiment with a pre-registered invalidation threshold, the activation metric read, the chosen path (build/pivot/kill), the rejected path, and a reviewer objection. A peer reads it and can restate which assumption you were testing without you narrating.
customer-discovery.unlock: Your packet names one falsifiable assumption, sets the invalidation threshold before the data, and the decision follows the evidence — not your enthusiasm.
customer-discovery.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'validated demand' because interviews felt encouraging. Compliments are not evidence. If your questions could only produce a YES — 'Wouldn't it be great if…' — that is confirmation theater, not discovery. Discovery is only real when a NO was possible and you set the kill line in advance.

customer-discovery.text: The team spent four months building the feature everyone in the room loved — and shipped it to silence: 2% activation, retention flat. In the retro, one line lands: nobody had ever asked a customer to do the thing before they built the thing.

Customer discovery is the cheapest experiment you will ever run: it converts 'we think users want this' into evidence a reviewer can inspect before engineering spends a sprint. It is the front of the product feedback loop — discovery feeds the PRD, the PRD scopes the build, and the activation metric closes the loop back to whether the assumption was true.

customer-discovery.prompt: You interview ten target customers and eight say 'yes, I'd definitely use that.' Is your idea validated? Decide before reading on.
customer-discovery.reveal: No — you learned almost nothing. 'Would you use it' asks people to predict their future behavior and be polite, and they fail at both. A YES to a hypothetical costs the customer nothing. Real discovery asks about PAST behavior ('walk me through the last time you hit this problem — what did you do?') and, better, asks for a commitment now: a pre-order, a signup, a calendar hold. Eight cheerful yeses to a hypothetical is the exact signal that precedes a 2% activation launch.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Context & market segment
- Idea: one-click bulk invoice export for solo bookkeepers
- Segment: freelance bookkeepers, 5-40 clients, on our free tier

## Riskiest assumption (falsifiable)
- They will change their monthly workflow to use OUR export instead of manual CSV

## Discovery interviews (past behavior, not hypotheticals)

# Writing the decision packet, one section at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real product idea you are tempted to build and run customer discovery on it FIRST: turn a risky assumption into an interview + experiment, read the activation/retention signal, and write the decision packet that says build, pivot, or kill — with the invalidation threshold set BEFORE you look at the data.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only score_interviews at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Point to the single riskiest assumption. If it's 'people want this,' sharpen it to the specific belief that, if false, kills the idea.
# 2. Read your interview questions aloud. If any one of them can only produce a YES, rewrite it to probe PAST behavior or ask for a real commitment.
# 3. Find the invalidation threshold and confirm it was written BEFORE the data. A threshold set after the result is a rationalization — mark it and redo.
# 4. Confirm the metric is behavioral (activation, retention, conversion), not attitudinal ('they liked it').
# 5. Check the decision (build/pivot/kill) actually follows the signal against the threshold — even where it contradicts what the team hoped.
# 6. Confirm a reviewer objection is written and answered — the strongest argument against your own read.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

    {"unprompted_pain": True,  "pays_for_workaround": False, "polite_yes": True},

    {"unprompted_pain": True,  "pays_for_workaround": True,  "polite_yes": True},
    {"unprompted_pain": True,  "pays_for_workaround": False, "polite_yes": True},
    {"unprompted_pain": False, "pays_for_workaround": False, "polite_yes": True},
]
RULE_UNPROMPTED = 7
RULE_WORKAROUND = 5


def score_interviews(interviews):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

n = len(INTERVIEWS)
u, w, p = score_interviews(INTERVIEWS)
print(f"n={n} interviews")
print(f"unprompted pain: {u}/{n}")
print(f"pays for a workaround today: {w}/{n}")
print(f"polite yes (worth zero as evidence): {p}/{n}")
print(f"pre-registered rule: unprompted>={RULE_UNPROMPTED} AND workaround>={RULE_WORKAROUND}")
if u >= RULE_UNPROMPTED and w >= RULE_WORKAROUND:
    print("verdict: CONTINUE - evidence clears both bars")
else:
    misses = []
    if u < RULE_UNPROMPTED:
        misses.append(f"unprompted {u}<{RULE_UNPROMPTED}")
    if w < RULE_WORKAROUND:
        misses.append(f"workaround {w}<{RULE_WORKAROUND}")
    print(f"verdict: DO NOT BUILD - {', '.join(misses)}")

customer-discovery.subtitle: Riskiest assumption → discovery interviews → experiment with a pre-set invalidation threshold → activation/retention signal → decision. The failure path (confirmation questions → false YES → build → dead launch) is drawn so you can see it before you live it.

storyboard.say: It starts here: name the single riskiest assumption — the belief that, if wrong, kills the whole feature.
You test that belief with discovery interviews — talking to real customers before writing any code.
Interviews feed an experiment, and here is the invariant: you pre-set the invalidation threshold before you see any data.
The experiment measures real behavior — activation and retention — the only signal that can honestly say yes or no.
Compare that signal against the threshold you locked in, and the decision makes itself — enthusiasm can't move the goalposts.
Now the failure path. The tempting shortcut skips the experiment and jumps straight to confirmation questions.
Those questions ask for a yes, so you get a false yes — approval with no evidence a customer will actually do the thing.
Build on that vibe and you ship to silence: a dead launch. Nobody had asked a customer to act before the team built it.

customer-discovery.text: The senior product tell: set the invalidation threshold BEFORE you see the data, and say it out loud in the room. 'If activation is under 30%, we kill this' pre-commits you to the evidence. Teams that set the kill line after the results always find a reason the results don't count — which is why they ship 2% launches. This discipline is exactly what the NIST AI RMF calls for: decisions gated on measured signal, not on confidence. (It also echoes DORA's broader principle of measuring delivery outcomes rather than asserting them.)

customer-discovery.question: A reviewer says: 'Show me the exact evidence that this discovery isn't just a happy-path answer.' Which packet element proves it?
options: A slide showing 8 of 10 interviewees said they liked the idea.
An activation metric read against an invalidation threshold that was written down before the data, with the decision (pivot) following the number even though the team was excited.
A long transcript of enthusiastic customer quotes.
A roadmap showing the feature scheduled for next sprint.
customer-discovery.explanation: Only option 2 shows falsifiability in action: a threshold set before the data (so it couldn't be moved), a behavioral metric (activation, not opinion), and a decision that overrode the team's enthusiasm because the number said so. Liked-it slides (1), quote reels (3), and roadmaps (4) all survive whether or not the idea is real — they carry no NO.

A reviewer agrees the wedge is defensible and the invalidation threshold is real.
competitive-landscape.unlock: Your landscape names the real alternatives (including 'do nothing'), isolates one wedge for a named market segment, and ties it to a falsifiable experiment with an invalidation threshold.
competitive-landscape.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a competitive landscape if it is a feature-comparison grid of you vs three logos. A checklist of who has SSO tells a reviewer nothing about which customer switches and why. The landscape is a claim about where a segment is underserved — and a bet you can invalidate — not a scorecard where you conveniently win every row.

competitive-landscape.text: The deck says 'we have no real competitors.' A staff PM asks one question — 'so what does your target customer use today at 4pm on a Tuesday when this problem hits?' — and the honest answer is a spreadsheet, a Slack thread, and a competitor's free tier. That is the landscape, and it was invisible because nobody looked past the logos.

This lesson sits in the foundation phase of Product Execution And Market Feedback: it turns problem framing and customer discovery into a build decision. The landscape is the section of your decision packet that converts 'the market is crowded' into 'this segment is underserved on this axis, and here is the experiment that proves it' — the bridge from market evidence to scoped engineering.

competitive-landscape.prompt: You list your three closest competitors and win most of the feature-comparison rows. Are you ready to build? Decide before reading on.
competitive-landscape.reveal: No — you counted the wrong competitors. Your real rival is usually the 'do nothing' option and the janky substitute (a spreadsheet, an intern, a free tier), because that is what your customer actually uses today. Winning a feature grid against three named tools means nothing if the segment you target is happily doing nothing. The landscape is not 'who else sells software' — it is 'what does this customer currently hire to solve this job, and why would they fire it for you?'

competitive-landscape.code:
## Competitive Landscape
- Job to be done: get a new hire productive in a tool on day one
- Target segment: 5-person ops teams at seed-stage startups (no admin)
- Alternatives they hire today:
  - Incumbent: EnterpriseSuite ($40/seat, 2-week setup, needs an admin)
  - Substitute: a shared spreadsheet + a Slack onboarding thread
  - Do nothing: new hire figures it out, ~3 days of lost output
- Wedge (segment x unmet axis): self-serve setup in < 10 min, no admin
- Experiment: 20 seed-stage ops leads, concierge onboarding, measure time-to-first-value

# Mission: Take one real product idea and map its competitive landscape into a decision that changes what you build next: name the incumbents and substitutes, find the one wedge where a market segment is underserved, and commit the finding — with customer evidence — to a reviewable packet, not a note.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only best_coverage at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Point to a named market segment specific enough to interview, not 'the market' or 'teams'. If you cannot recruit 20 of them, it is too vague.

}

}

    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.

    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

storyboard.say: Start with the target segment. The whole landscape is a hiring question: what can these customers hire for this job today?
The named incumbent is one option, but for this segment it is too costly, so it rarely gets the job.
The real rivals hide in plain sight: a substitute they hire today, and doing nothing, which often wins at 4pm on a Tuesday.
Now find the wedge: the one axis where this segment stays underserved by every alternative on the board.
That wedge is not a slogan. It becomes a bet: a scoped experiment you can actually build and run.
The experiment names an activation metric it must move, converting market evidence into a measurable target.
And it carries an invalidation threshold. If that bar is missed, the bet dies. The invariant: it must be able to fail.

value-proposition.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'validated the value prop' because customers said they liked it. Stated interest is not evidence — a value prop is validated only when a behavioral experiment cleared a pre-committed threshold. Approval with no threshold is theater.

value-proposition.text: Two teams ship the same feature. One asked five customers 'would you use this?', heard yes, built for a quarter, and launched to silence. The other ran a $200 fake-door test, watched 3% click where they needed 15%, and killed it in a week — saving the quarter. Same idea; one had a value proposition, the other had a wish.

A value proposition sits in the foundation phase of product execution: it's the bridge from customer discovery to a scoped build. Get it right and every later artifact — PRD, MVP scope, metric tree, launch — inherits a defensible target; get it wrong and you instrument a feature nobody's job needs.

value-proposition.reveal: It names no one and risks nothing. 'Faster, easier' is true of every product ever pitched, for a segment of 'everyone', against a job that was never specified. There's nothing to falsify — no experiment can return 'no'. A real value prop is dangerous: 'For freelance designers who dread month-end, we cut invoice chase from 40 min to 5 — and we're betting they'll pay $12/mo to never chase again.' That last clause is a claim reality can kill.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Value Proposition
- Segment: freelance designers billing 5-15 clients/month
- Job-to-be-done: stop chasing overdue invoices (currently ~40 min/wk of dread)
- Value claim: auto-chase + one-tap reminders; they never manually chase again
- Riskiest assumption: they will PAY $12/mo to remove the chase (not just want it free)

## Experiment (must be able to return "no")
- Design: fake-door pricing page + concierge onboarding for first 20 sign-ups
- Activation metric: paid-checkout starts / unique visitors from the discovery list
- Invalidation threshold: < 15% start checkout OR < 8 of 20 complete concierge -> assumption false
- Run window: 10 business days, traffic capped at 300 visitors

## Decision Memo
- Selected approach: build MVP only if threshold cleared
- Rejected approach: build first, monetize later (defers the riskiest bet, burns a quarter)
- Reversal condition: if retention < 40% at day 30, the value prop is 'nice-to-have', re-open
- Expected failure: interest is high, willingness-to-PAY is low (the classic vitamin-not-painkiller trap)
- Capstone link: this segment + threshold seed the PRD, metric tree, and launch feedback report
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
Name the segment, not 'users': 'Freelance designers billing 5-15 clients/mo' is reachable and homogeneous. 'Small businesses' cannot be interviewed, tested, or sized — it's a segment of one word.
State the job-to-be-done: Customers hire products to make progress on a job. Name the pain and quantify it (~40 min/wk of dread) so the value is measurable, not adjectival.

Isolate the riskiest assumption: Not 'does the feature work' — 'will they PAY to remove the chase'. Willingness-to-pay is usually the assumption most likely to be false and most expensive to discover late.
Design an experiment that can fail: A fake-door + concierge produces BEHAVIOR (clicks, completions), not stated intent. If it can only say 'they liked it', it is not an experiment.

Pre-commit the invalidation threshold: < 15% checkout starts OR < 8/20 concierge completions kills the assumption. Committing the bar BEFORE the data is the whole discipline — it stops you rationalizing a miss into a win.

Write the decision, its reversal, and the expected failure: Chosen vs rejected with a reversal condition (retention < 40% re-opens it). Naming the expected failure — vitamin, not painkiller — is what a reviewer inspects for honesty.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

# Mission: Take one real (or realistic) product idea you might build, and write a Value Proposition that is testable — a named customer segment, the job/pain it addresses, and the ONE assumption that, if false, kills the idea — then attach the falsifying experiment and its invalidation threshold.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only value_multiple at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your segment aloud. If you could not build a list of 20 real people or accounts to test it on, it's too broad — narrow it until you can.
# 2. Point to the single riskiest assumption. If it's 'does the feature work' rather than 'will this segment change behavior / pay', you've named the safe assumption, not the risky one.
# 3. Confirm the experiment can return 'no': write the exact result that would falsify the assumption. If no result can falsify it, it's a demo, not an experiment.
# 4. Check the invalidation threshold was committed BEFORE data collection and is a behavioral metric (activation, checkout, retention) — not stated interest.
# 5. Confirm the decision memo names the rejected option and a reversal condition, so the choice is defensible under review, not just asserted.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

    "freelance-designers": (1.5, 40.0),
    "small-agencies":      (0.5, 60.0),
    "hobby-sellers":       (0.3, 20.0),
}
PRICE = 29.0
BAR = 3.0


def value_multiple(hours_per_week, hourly_rate, price):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

passing = []
for seg in sorted(SEGMENTS):
    h, r = SEGMENTS[seg]
    value, mult = value_multiple(h, r, PRICE)
    verdict = "PASS" if mult >= BAR else "FAIL"
    if mult >= BAR:
        passing.append((mult, seg))
    print(f"{seg}: value ${value:.0f}/mo vs ${PRICE:.0f} -> {mult:.1f}x {verdict}")
best = max(passing)
print(f"beachhead: {best[1]} at {best[0]:.1f}x")

storyboard.say: Start with the segment: name one market you serve, and the specific job it hires you for. That job is the whole reason the product exists.
The job exposes the bet — the single riskiest assumption that, if false, sinks the entire idea no matter how well you build it.
Here's the invariant: that assumption must be wireable to an experiment designed to falsify it — a test whose 'no' can actually stop the build.
The experiment produces real behavior, which becomes an activation metric — like clicks on a fake-door test, not a survey's polite yes.
That metric is measured against the invalidation threshold: the bar you set in advance. This is the fork — clear it or miss it.
Clear the bar and you earn the right to build: scope the MVP with a defensible target every later artifact inherits.
Miss the bar and you pivot or kill — the failure path. Three percent clicked where you needed fifteen; you saved the quarter.
The repair loop is the lesson: a failed threshold sends you back to reframe the segment or assumption — never to quietly relax the bar.

value-proposition.code:
# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Value Proposition
- Segment: freelance designers billing 5-15 clients/month
- Job-to-be-done: stop chasing overdue invoices (currently ~40 min/wk of dread)
- Value claim: auto-chase + one-tap reminders; they never manually chase again
- Riskiest assumption: they will PAY $12/mo to remove the chase (not just want it free)

## Experiment (must be able to return "no")
- Design: fake-door pricing page + concierge onboarding for first 20 sign-ups
- Activation metric: paid-checkout starts / unique visitors from the discovery list
- Invalidation threshold: < 15% start checkout OR < 8 of 20 complete concierge -> assumption false
- Run window: 10 business days, traffic capped at 300 visitors

## Decision Memo
- Selected approach: build MVP only if threshold cleared
- Rejected approach: build first, monetize later (defers the riskiest bet, burns a quarter)
- Reversal condition: if retention < 40% at day 30, the value prop is 'nice-to-have', re-open
- Expected failure: interest is high, willingness-to-PAY is low (the classic vitamin-not-painkiller trap)
- Capstone link: this segment + threshold seed the PRD, metric tree, and launch feedback report

steps.label: Name the segment, not 'users'
steps.note: 'Freelance designers billing 5-15 clients/mo' is reachable and homogeneous. 'Small businesses' cannot be interviewed, tested, or sized — it's a segment of one word.

steps.label: State the job-to-be-done
steps.note: Customers hire products to make progress on a job. Name the pain and quantify it (~40 min/wk of dread) so the value is measurable, not adjectival.

steps.label: Isolate the riskiest assumption
steps.note: Not 'does the feature work' — 'will they PAY to remove the chase'. Willingness-to-pay is usually the assumption most likely to be false and most expensive to discover late.

steps.label: Design an experiment that can fail
steps.note: A fake-door + concierge produces BEHAVIOR (clicks, completions), not stated intent. If it can only say 'they liked it', it is not an experiment.

steps.label: Pre-commit the invalidation threshold
steps.note: < 15% checkout starts OR < 8/20 concierge completions kills the assumption. Committing the bar BEFORE the data is the whole discipline — it stops you rationalizing a miss into a win.

steps.label: Write the decision, its reversal, and the expected failure
steps.note: Chosen vs rejected with a reversal condition (retention < 40% re-opens it). Naming the expected failure — vitamin, not painkiller — is what a reviewer inspects for honesty.

options: "Every customer we interviewed said they loved the idea and would use it."
"We ran a fake-door test against our target segment; 9% of visitors started checkout versus a pre-committed 15% threshold — so we killed the paid version and re-opened the free-tier assumption."

"We're confident the market is huge, so the value prop must be strong."

user-journey.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'validated the journey' if your experiment can only return good news. A survey that asks 'would you use this?' confirms; it cannot invalidate. If no result could stop the build, you drew a happy path, not a User Journey.

user-journey.text: The demo lands, the room nods, and the founder greenlights a three-month build — nobody in the room can say which single step a real customer takes before they'd pay, or where they'd quietly abandon. Six weeks later the funnel says what the journey never asked: users never reached the feature at all.

A User Journey is the ordered set of steps a real customer takes from first trigger to activation — the reviewable spine that connects market evidence to a scoped build decision. It sits at the front of Module 2: everything downstream (PRD, MVP scope, instrumentation, experiments, launch) is only as honest as the journey it's built on.

user-journey.prompt: "Users will love this because it saves them time." Before you build it — what's wrong with that as a journey? Answer before reading on.
user-journey.reveal: It's a happy path with no steps and no exit. A real User Journey names each move a customer makes (trigger → discover → first value → habit) and, at every move, the reason they'd drop. 'They'll love it' skips straight to activation and never asks who is doing what, in what order, and where the friction is. The invariant of a journey: it must contain the step where the customer LEAVES, not just the step where they win.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Journey (trigger -> activation)
trigger: solo founder needs weekly revenue view -> discover -> sign up -> [SETUP: connect Stripe] -> first value: sees dashboard

## Suspect step + assumption
Suspect step: Setup (connect Stripe). Assumption: >=60% who sign up finish the connect step within one session.

## Activation metric + invalidation threshold
Metric: activation = % of signups reaching "first dashboard" same session.
Invalidation threshold: if activation < 40% over 30 signups, the build path is DEAD.

## Experiment (must be able to fail)
Fake-door + concierge onboarding: 30 real signups, manual connect offered mid-flow; measure who reaches first value.

## Rejected build path
Rejected: build full self-serve OAuth connector first. Why: bets 3 weeks before the drop-off is even measured.

## Expected failure / reviewer objection
Expected failure: setup friction, not value, kills activation. Objection: "survey said they'd use it" is not activation evidence.

## Capstone connection
Feeds the capstone: this journey + threshold becomes the instrumentation + experiment section of the product feedback report.
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
The journey line: Ordered steps, trigger to activation, no solution smuggled in. The [SETUP] bracket marks the step you fear — everything hangs on it.
Suspect step + assumption: One named step, one falsifiable assumption with a number (>=60%). 'Users will love it' has no step and no number — it can't be tested.
Activation metric + invalidation threshold: The threshold is the whole skill: <40% over 30 signups KILLS the build. A metric with no kill-number is a vanity metric.
The experiment: Concierge/fake-door measures real behavior at the suspect step. It must be able to return 'no one activated' — a confirm-only test is theater.
The rejected path: Naming what you did NOT build (full OAuth connector first) proves you chose evidence over momentum.
Failure autopsy + capstone: Predict the failure (friction, not value) and wire the artifact into the capstone feedback report — reusable, not a one-off note.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

# Writing the decision packet, one field at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real product idea you are tempted to build and turn it into a User Journey you can test: map the customer's steps from trigger to activation, mark the ONE step where you believe they'll drop, and design the smallest experiment whose result could kill your assumption before you write a line of build code.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only step_conversions at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your journey aloud. If it's one step ('they'll love it') instead of an ordered trigger→activation sequence, it's a wish — decompose it into the real moves.
# 2. Point to the ONE suspect step where you fear the customer drops. If you can't name it, you drew only the happy path.
# 3. Check your activation metric is behavioral (did they reach first value?), not attitudinal (did they say they liked it?).
# 4. Confirm the invalidation threshold is a concrete number over a concrete sample — the line that, if missed, kills the build path.
# 5. Confirm your experiment can return 'no one activated'. A test that can only confirm your idea is theater — redesign it.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

FUNNEL = [
    ("trigger", 1000),
    ("discover", 620),
    ("signup", 240),
    ("setup-stripe-connect", 90),
    ("first-value", 60),
]
KILL_LINE = 20.0


def step_conversions(funnel):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

convs = step_conversions(FUNNEL)
for step, c in convs:
    print(f"{step}: {c * 100:.1f}% convert ({100 - c * 100:.1f}% drop)")
worst = min(convs, key=lambda x: x[1])
print(f"feared step confirmed: {worst[0]} loses {100 - worst[1] * 100:.1f}%")
counts = dict(FUNNEL)
activation = counts["first-value"] / counts["signup"] * 100
verdict = "JOURNEY HOLDS" if activation >= KILL_LINE else "RESCOPE"
print(f"activation (first-value/signup): {activation:.1f}%")
print(f"kill-line {KILL_LINE:.1f}%: {verdict}")

# 2. Point to the ONE suspect step where you fear the customer drops. If you can't name it, you drew only the happy path.
# 3. Check your activation metric is behavioral (did they reach first value?), not attitudinal (did they say they liked it?).

    ("discover", 620),
    ("signup", 240),
    ("setup-stripe-connect", 90),
    ("first-value", 60),
]
KILL_LINE = 20.0

convs = step_conversions(FUNNEL)
for step, c in convs:

storyboard.say: It starts with a trigger. A real customer arrives with a job to do, then discovers the product.
They commit by signing up, then get onboarded into setup — the first real friction of the journey.
Setup is the suspect step: the one decision point where you fear the customer will quietly leak out of the funnel.
The win path is that setup activates them — they reach first value, the moment the product actually pays off.
But the feared path is real too: at setup they drop and abandon, never reaching the feature at all.
Abandonment triggers a test — you instrument the leak and run an experiment against the suspect step.
The experiment loops back to setup: it either invalidates your guess or repairs the step so activation holds.
The invariant: a journey holds the exit, not just the win. No measurable drop-off means you drew a demo.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Journey (trigger -> activation)
trigger: solo founder needs weekly revenue view -> discover -> sign up -> [SETUP: connect Stripe] -> first value: sees dashboard

## Suspect step + assumption
Suspect step: Setup (connect Stripe). Assumption: >=60% who sign up finish the connect step within one session.

## Activation metric + invalidation threshold
Metric: activation = % of signups reaching "first dashboard" same session.
Invalidation threshold: if activation < 40% over 30 signups, the build path is DEAD.

## Experiment (must be able to fail)
Fake-door + concierge onboarding: 30 real signups, manual connect offered mid-flow; measure who reaches first value.

## Rejected build path
Rejected: build full self-serve OAuth connector first. Why: bets 3 weeks before the drop-off is even measured.

## Expected failure / reviewer objection
Expected failure: setup friction, not value, kills activation. Objection: "survey said they'd use it" is not activation evidence.

## Capstone connection
Feeds the capstone: this journey + threshold becomes the instrumentation + experiment section of the product feedback report.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Assumption (from discovery)
Users churn in week 1 because setup is manual; a guided onboarding wizard will lift activation.

## Hypothesis (falsifiable)
Cohorts routed through the wizard reach activation ("first project shared") at a higher rate than control.

## Decision metric (ONE)
Day-7 activation rate = % of new signups who share a first project within 7 days.

## Invalidation threshold (pre-registered, set BEFORE data)
Cut the build if wizard-cohort D7 activation is < +5pp over control after 400 signups/arm.

## Rejected alternative
Measure raw signups — rejected: rises on marketing spend, cannot isolate the wizard.

## Stop rule
400 signups/arm reached OR 14 days elapsed → read the metric and DECIDE. No peeking-and-extending.

Falsifiable hypothesis: One variable (the wizard), a comparison to control. If it cannot come out 'no', it is not a hypothesis — it is a plan.
ONE decision metric: Activation defined operationally ('first project shared in 7 days'), not 'engagement'. One metric decides; a dashboard of ten decides nothing.
The invalidation threshold: The number that kills the build — +5pp, 400/arm — written BEFORE the data. This line is the entire skill; without it you will rationalize any result.
Rejected alternative: Name the vanity metric you refused and why. Raw signups move with ad spend and would let the wizard take false credit.
The stop rule: A concrete sample OR time box, and an explicit 'no peeking-and-extending'. Moving the goalposts mid-test is how teams p-hack themselves into a bad build.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

# Writing the decision packet, one line at a time
#
# Mission: Take one product assumption you are about to build on and design an experiment against it: write the customer_experiment_and_metric_decision_packet.md — the assumption, the one activation or retention metric that decides it, the exact invalidation threshold that would make you NOT build, and the cheapest test that reaches it.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only evaluate_experiment at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Point to the single decision metric. If you named more than one, you have no decision rule — pick the one that would change the build.
# 2. Read the invalidation threshold aloud. If it is not a number set BEFORE data, or if no realistic result could hit it, it cannot kill the build — fix it.
# 3. Confirm the metric isolates the change: is there a control or baseline, or could ad spend / seasonality move it instead of your feature?
# 4. Check the stop rule has a concrete sample size OR time box, plus 'no peeking-and-extending' — otherwise the threshold is negotiable.
# 5. Name the rejected vanity metric and why. If you cannot name what you refused to measure, you have not chosen — you defaulted.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

ARMS = {
    "control": (52, 200),
    "variant": (68, 200),
}
MIN_N = 200
DECISION_BAR = 32.0


def evaluate_experiment(arms):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

for name in sorted(ARMS):
    a, t = ARMS[name]
    if t < MIN_N:
        print(f"sample gate FAILED: {name} has {t} < {MIN_N} - no read allowed")
        raise SystemExit
rates = evaluate_experiment(ARMS)
for name in sorted(rates):
    a, t = ARMS[name]
    print(f"{name}: {a}/{t} = {rates[name]:.1f}%")
lift = rates["variant"] - rates["control"]
print(f"lift: {lift:+.1f}pp")
verdict = "BUILD" if rates["variant"] >= DECISION_BAR else "KILL"
print(f"pre-registered bar {DECISION_BAR:.1f}%: {verdict}")

experiment-design.subtitle: Discovery assumption → falsifiable hypothesis → one decision metric → measure against a PRE-SET invalidation threshold. The threshold gate is the whole skill: it can return 'no' and stop the build. Vanity signups are deliberately out of scope.

storyboard.say: It starts as an assumption — 'users are asking for team workspaces.' That's a hallway opinion, not yet something you can be wrong about.
First move: sharpen the assumption into a falsifiable hypothesis — a claim that could actually turn out false against real data.
Then bind the hypothesis to exactly ONE decision metric — activation or retention — so the result can't be argued after the fact.
Guard that metric hard: vanity signups must NOT leak in. Signups feel like progress but they never tell you the feature worked.
Now measure the metric against the invalidation threshold — a kill-number you commit to in advance, before any data lands.
This gate is the whole skill. Land below the line and it returns 'no' — you cut the build instead of shipping six wasted weeks.
Land above it and the evidence earns the scope — now you build, connecting discovery to a decision you can defend.
The invariant: the kill-number is set before the data. That's what turns 'users want this' into a decision, not a hope.

experiment-design.caption: The tell is falsifiability: if no result stops the build, you measured activity to feel busy, not truth to decide.

experiment-design.text: Pros pre-register the kill-number in the packet before the experiment runs (in the spirit of NIST AI RMF's MEASURE function, which calls for defined metrics and acceptance criteria set for the deployment context). (Note: 'measure against a threshold you set in advance' is not a NIST RMF quote; do not attribute it as one.) Deciding the threshold after seeing the data is how a flat result gets narrated into a launch — the human bias the pre-commitment exists to defeat. If your threshold moved once the numbers arrived, you ran a rationalization, not an experiment.

experiment-design.question: Which of these is a real experiment design rather than a launch wearing a lab coat?
options: "Ship the new pricing page and watch revenue — if it grows, it worked."
"Route 50% of signups through the wizard; if D7 activation isn't at least +5pp over control after 400/arm, we cut it — decided before we start."
"Add the referral feature because three interviews asked for it."
"Launch to everyone, then check engagement dashboards and see how it feels."
experiment-design.explanation: Only option 2 pre-registers ONE decision metric (D7 activation vs a control), a falsifiable invalidation threshold (+5pp), and a stop rule (400/arm) — a result that can return 'no' and cut the build. The others measure vanity metrics with no control (1, 4) or skip measurement entirely (3), so no data could ever stop them.

Confirm the metric isolates the change: is there a control or baseline, or could ad spend / seasonality move it instead of your feature?
Check the stop rule has a concrete sample size OR time box, plus 'no peeking-and-extending' — otherwise the threshold is negotiable.
Name the rejected vanity metric and why. If you cannot name what you refused to measure, you have not chosen — you defaulted.

mvp-scope.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have 'scoped an MVP' if your scope is 'build the whole thing, but v1'. That is a smaller build, not a scoped experiment. An MVP scope is defined by the assumption it tests and the threshold that would stop it — not by feature count.

mvp-scope.text: The roadmap says 'build the marketplace'; the founder wants payments, reviews, chat, and search by launch. A staff PM asks one question — 'What is the single thing that has to be true, or none of this matters?' — and the room goes quiet, because everyone scoped features and nobody scoped the bet.

MVP scoping sits in the applied phase of the product loop: it turns 'we could build a lot' into 'we will test the one assumption that gates everything else.' The output is not a feature list — it is a customer experiment with an activation metric and an invalidation threshold, Section 1 of the decision packet you defend in review.

mvp-scope.prompt: "Our MVP is the full product, just with fewer features." Before you cut the feature list — what is wrong with that as an MVP scope? Answer before reading on.
mvp-scope.reveal: It scopes the BUILD, not the BET. 'Fewer features' still assumes the product is worth building and just trims cost; it never asks which assumption, if false, makes the whole thing worthless. A real MVP scope names the riskiest assumption ('users will connect their bank to a stranger's app'), designs the cheapest experiment that could return 'no', and picks one activation metric — e.g. '40% of signups complete a first booking in 7 days.' The feature-trim MVP feels like discipline while quietly betting the entire idea is sound.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## 1. Context
- Idea: peer-to-peer tool rental in one zip code
- Decision: build the booking flow, or run a concierge test first?

## 2. Riskiest assumption (if false, the idea dies)
- Owners will lend a $400 tool to a stranger for $12/day

## 3. Selected experiment (cheapest falsifier)
- Concierge: we broker 20 rentals by hand via a landing page + SMS
- Rejected scope: full app w/ payments, chat, reviews, search

## 4. Activation metric + invalidation threshold
- Metric: % of listed tools that complete >=1 real rental in 14 days
- Keep going if: >= 30%   |   Invalidate / pivot if: < 15%

## 5. Expected failure
- Owners list, but ghost on first booking request (trust gap)

## 6. Verification method
- Interview notes (10 owners) + rental log + funnel: list -> request -> handoff

## 7. Reviewer objection
- "30% of 20 is noise." Response: threshold is directional, not powered; a 3/20 result still kills the trust bet cheaply.
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
Context, no solution in it: State the idea and the actual decision (concierge vs build). If this section already lists features, you scoped the build, not the bet.
The riskiest assumption: One sentence a skeptic could bet against. 'Owners lend to strangers' is riskier than 'the UI is usable' — test the thing most likely to be false.
Cheapest experiment + rejected scope: Concierge (hand-broker 20 rentals) beats building payments. Naming the REJECTED bigger scope proves you cut on purpose, not by omission.
One activation metric + a numeric threshold: '% of listed tools with >=1 real rental' is activation, not a vanity signup count. The <15% invalidation line is what makes this a bet you can lose.
Expected failure: Name the realistic failure mode (owners ghost on first request) so a 'no' result is interpretable, not a shrug.
Verification method: Interview notes + rental log + funnel. Evidence a reviewer can inspect, not a feeling that 'people seemed interested'.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

# Writing the decision packet, one line at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real (or realistic) product idea you are tempted to build, and scope the smallest MVP that can EARN the right to be built. Write the scope decision as customer_experiment_and_metric_decision_packet.md: the riskiest assumption, the one experiment that could kill it, the single activation metric that says 'keep going', and the invalidation threshold that says 'stop'.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only rank_scopes at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your riskiest assumption aloud. If a skeptic would nod along ('sure, that's obviously true'), it is not risky — find the one they'd bet against.
# 2. Check your experiment can return 'no'. If every outcome means 'keep building', it is a demo, not a test — redesign it.
# 3. Confirm the activation metric measures first VALUE (a completed core action), not signups or clicks. Vanity metrics only go up.
# 4. Confirm the invalidation threshold is a NUMBER. 'If it does badly' is not a threshold; '< 15% in 14 days' is.
# 5. List what you scoped OUT (payments, chat, reviews...) and defend each omission: it is not needed to test THIS assumption.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

SCOPES = [
    ("full-marketplace-app", 45, 5, True),
    ("booking-flow-only", 20, 2, False),
    ("landing-page-waitlist", 2, 1, True),
    ("concierge-30-owner-calls", 3, 4, True),
]
KILL_LINE = "fewer than 8 of 30 owners list a tool -> STOP"


def rank_scopes(scopes):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

excluded = [s[0] for s in SCOPES if not s[3]]
for name in excluded:
    print(f"excluded: {name} (cannot return a NO on the riskiest assumption)")
ranked = rank_scopes(SCOPES)
for name, spd in ranked:
    print(f"{name}: {spd:.2f} signal/day")
winner = ranked[0]
print(f"chosen scope: {winner[0]}")
print(f"registered kill-line: {KILL_LINE}")
mvp-scope.check:
excluded: booking-flow-only (cannot return a NO on the riskiest assumption)
concierge-30-owner-calls: 1.33 signal/day
landing-page-waitlist: 0.50 signal/day
full-marketplace-app: 0.11 signal/day
chosen scope: concierge-30-owner-calls
registered kill-line: fewer than 8 of 30 owners list a tool -> STOP

storyboard.say: We start with a product idea. The trap: scope the feature list. The move: don't build yet — interrogate the bet underneath.
First, isolate the one riskiest assumption — the single thing that, if false, sinks the whole idea.
Now design the cheapest experiment that can actually falsify it — a test whose honest answer is allowed to be no.
Everything else — payments, chat, reviews, search — is out of scope, and it must not leak into the experiment.
The experiment measures one activation metric, compared against a numeric threshold you commit to in advance.
At or above threshold, the bet held — double down and keep building.
Below threshold, you stop. Invalidate or pivot — no rationalizing, no shipping the roadmap anyway.
The invariant: scope tests the bet, never the feature list. That's Section one of the packet you defend in review.

prd-rfc.code:
# PRD/RFC — Post-checkout upsell decision packet

## 1. Context + segment
Segment: returning buyers, 2+ orders/90d (34% of revenue)
Signal: 9/12 discovery interviews said "I'd add a matching item if asked at checkout"

## 2. Assumptions (each falsifiable)
- A1: intent exists AT checkout, not just in interviews
- A2: an upsell won't depress checkout conversion (feared failure)

## 3. Selected approach (smallest build)
One-item contextual upsell on the confirmation step. 1 sprint, flag-gated A/B.

## 4. Rejected approach
Full recommendation carousel — 4 sprints; over-builds before A2 is tested.

## 5. Metric tree
North star: revenue/visitor
  activation: upsell-attach-rate (leaf we move)
  guardrail: checkout-conversion (must not drop)
  retention: 30d repeat-purchase (secondary)

## 6. Expected failure
Attach-rate looks good BUT checkout-conversion drops 2pts — net-negative revenue.

## 7. Verification + invalidation threshold
A/B, 2 wks, 95% power on attach-rate.
SHIP if attach ≥ 8% AND conversion delta ≥ -0.5pt.
KILL if conversion drops > 1pt at any point (guardrail trips).

## 8. Reviewer objection
"Interviews are stated preference; attach-rate is the only real proof." — logged.

## 9. Repair notes + capstone connection
Repair: added the conversion guardrail after review caught A2 untested.
Feeds capstone: discovery → PRD → instrumentation → experiment → launch → feedback report.

# Writing the decision packet, one section at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real product idea you want to ship and write the PRD/RFC as a reviewable decision packet — not a doc that describes a feature, but one that ties customer evidence to a scoped build call: context, assumptions, the approach you chose, the approach you rejected, the failure you expect, and the invalidation threshold that would make you kill it.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only lint_packet at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your problem statement aloud. If it contains the build ("so we're building X"), you fused evidence and fix — split them into the discovery signal and the selected approach.
# 2. Point to the customer-discovery signal: is it a verbatim, counted signal from a named segment, or an unfalsifiable "users want"? If a reviewer can't inspect it, it isn't evidence.
# 3. Find your rejected approach. If there is only one path in the packet, you hid the tradeoff — name what you did NOT build and why.
# 4. Locate the invalidation threshold. It must be a number set BEFORE the experiment (SHIP if ≥ X, KILL if guardrail drops > Y). No number means no decision.
# 5. Check the metric tree has a guardrail, not just a metric to grow — the feared failure (e.g. conversion drop) must be instrumented, or you can only ever see good news.
#

## Metric tree
take_rate -> aov_lift -> weekly_revenue_per_buyer
## Decision
Proceed if review cannot break the rejected-option logic.
"""

    "Context",
    "Assumptions",
    "Selected approach",
    "Rejected approach",
    "Expected failure",
    "Verification method",
    "Metric tree",
    "Invalidation threshold",
    "Decision",
]

storyboard.say: The loop starts here: customer discovery is the raw signal, the real evidence that some market segment has a problem worth solving.
That signal flows into the PRD, where market evidence becomes a scoped engineering decision instead of a hunch on a roadmap.
Watch the trap: 'users want it' vibes try to sneak into the PRD, but conviction is not evidence and must never substitute for signal.
A real PRD names the metric, activation or retention, and the metric tree instruments the smallest experiment that can move it.
The experiment ships and reports its result against the invalidation threshold, the number set in advance that would prove the idea wrong.
The threshold is the gate: clear the bar and you ship; miss it and you loop back to re-discover instead of laundering advocacy.
The invariant: every decision carries a number that could kill it. No invalidation threshold means no decision, just advocacy.

metric-design.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'designed a metric' if the metric can only go up (signups, page views, total users). A metric with no failure direction proves nothing — it is a scoreboard for the happy path. A designed metric has a threshold below which the idea is dead.

metric-design.text: The launch review is going well: signups are up 40%, the deck is green, everyone is nodding. Then the staff PM asks, 'Of the people who signed up last month, how many came back in week two?' — and the room realizes nobody chose a metric that could ever say no.

A feedback loop is only as honest as the metric at its center: the wrong metric turns a failing product into a green dashboard. Metric Design is the move that connects a customer-discovery insight to one number your experiment can actually move — the hinge between market evidence and a scoped build decision.

metric-design.prompt: Your growth chart shows total registered users climbing steadily up and to the right. Is that a good activation metric? Decide before reading on.
metric-design.reveal: No — it is a vanity metric. Total registered users is cumulative: it can only rise, even while every new cohort churns out in a week. It cannot fall, so it can never tell you the product is failing. An activation metric measures whether a NEW user reaches value ('% of signups who complete a first order in 24h'), and a retention metric measures whether they come BACK ('% still active in week two'). Those can drop — which is exactly why they carry information.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## 1. Discovery insight (the evidence)
- Segment: new self-serve merchants, first 7 days
- Interview signal (n=9): 6 abandoned before their first order — checkout felt risky

## 2. Metric tree
- North Star: weekly repeat purchasers
  - Activation: % of signups with a first order within 24h   <- TARGET
  - Retention: % of activated users still active in week two
- Excluded (vanity): total signups — cumulative, cannot fall

## 3. The bet
- Target metric: 24h activation rate
- Baseline (current): 18%
- Target (this experiment): >= 28%
- Experiment: guided first-order checklist vs control, 2-week A/B

## 4. Invalidation threshold
- If activation stays <= 20% (inside noise of 18%), the insight is wrong → kill this bet
- Decision if it clears 28%: scope the checklist for GA
- Decision if 20–28%: iterate copy, re-test once, then drop
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
Ground it in discovery, not opinion: The metric comes FROM a customer insight — 6 of 9 interviews flagged checkout risk. Without this, you are decorating a guess with a number.
Decompose the North Star into a tree: One North Star (repeat purchasers) breaks into an activation input and a retention input. The tree is what makes the target metric a lever, not a floating stat.
Exclude the vanity metric on purpose: Naming total-signups as excluded is a judgment you defend, not an oversight. A cumulative metric can never invalidate anything.
One target metric, one baseline, one target: Pick the SINGLE metric the experiment moves. Baseline 18% + target 28% turns 'improve activation' into a falsifiable claim.
The invalidation threshold — the invariant: '<= 20% → the insight is wrong' is the line that can say NO. Set it inside the noise band of the baseline so a null result is unambiguous.
Pre-commit the decision: Clears → scope for GA. Muddy middle → one re-test then drop. Deciding the response BEFORE data removes the temptation to rationalize a green-looking miss.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

A reviewer can restate what you are betting on and what result would change your mind — without you narrating.

# Filling customer_experiment_and_metric_decision_packet.md, section by section
#
# Mission: Take one real product decision you are facing (or a realistic one) and design the metric that governs it: build a small metric tree from a North Star down to one activation and one retention metric, pick the single metric your next experiment will move, and set the invalidation threshold that would tell you the idea is wrong.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only leverage at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Point to the customer-discovery insight your target metric came from. If the metric floats free of any interview or usage signal, it is a guess with a number.
# 2. Confirm your target metric CAN fall. If it is cumulative (total signups, total views), replace it with a rate or a cohort metric that can drop.
# 3. Check you have exactly one target metric for this experiment — not five. Moving one lever keeps the result attributable.
# 4. Confirm a baseline AND a target exist, both numeric. 'Improve activation' with no numbers is not a bet.
# 5. Read your invalidation threshold aloud: does it name a specific result that would make you KILL the idea? If nothing could disprove the bet, it is theater.
# 6. Confirm the decision for each outcome (clear / muddy / miss) is pre-committed, so a green-looking miss cannot be rationalized after the fact.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

INPUTS = [
    ("signups_per_wk", 1200.0, 1300.0),
    ("activation_rate", 0.30, 0.40),
    ("w4_retention", 0.25, 0.30),
    ("projects_per_retained", 3.0, 3.2),
]


def north_star(values):
    out = 1.0
    for v in values:
        out *= v
    return out


def leverage(inputs):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

base = north_star([b for _, b, _ in INPUTS])
print(f"baseline north star: {base:.1f} weekly active projects")
rows = leverage(INPUTS)
for name, ns in rows:
    print(f"move {name} to target -> {ns:.1f} ({(ns / base - 1) * 100:+.1f}%)")
winner = max(rows, key=lambda r: r[1])
print(f"highest leverage: {winner[0]}")
print("threshold: onboarding rebuild must lift activation past 34% in 4 weeks or STOP")

instrumentation.text: The launch dashboard is all green — signups up, clicks up, the room is celebrating — and a week later retention craters, because the one event that would have shown users never reached the aha-moment was never fired. The team measured applause, not activation.

Instrumentation is the wire between a shipped feature and a real decision: no trustworthy events, no trustworthy feedback loop, and customer discovery collapses into opinion. This is Section built into the same decision packet you carry through experiments, launch, and the feedback report.

instrumentation.prompt: "Signups are up 40% since we launched onboarding v2 — ship it wider." Before you celebrate: what is wrong with signups as the metric that decides this? Answer before reading on.
instrumentation.reveal: Signups is a vanity metric sitting at the top of the funnel — it moves when marketing changes, not when the product works. The decision needs the ACTIVATION metric: did the new user reach the moment that predicts retention (e.g. 'created first project AND invited a teammate within 24h')? Signups can rise 40% while activation falls, and you'd scale a leak. The metric that decides must sit on the causal path to retention, not on the path to a press release.

instrumentation.code:
## Instrumentation Spec
event: user_activated
  props: { user_id, segment, ts, first_project_created: bool, teammate_invited: bool }
  fires_when: first_project_created == true AND teammate_invited == true, within 24h of signup
  fires_on_drop: emit user_activation_failed{user_id, last_step} at the 24h boundary

## Metric Tree (raw event -> north-star)
  signups                     (top of funnel, vanity)
   └─ activation_rate = activated / signups        <- THE decision metric
       └─ week1_retention (activated cohort)
           └─ NSM: weekly_active_teams

## Invalidation Threshold (pre-committed, before launch)
  activation_rate < 25% for the new-onboarding segment  ->  KILL v2, revert to v1
  fire-rate check: user_activated emitted for < 95% of eligible users -> instrumentation is broken, DECIDE NOTHING
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
Name the event + its schema: user_activated with typed props. 'we track activation' is a wish; a schema with user_id, segment, and ts is instrumentation a reviewer can inspect.
Define the aha-moment precisely: Activation is the AND of the two actions that predict retention — chosen from customer discovery, not from what was easy to log.
Instrument the DROP, not just the win: Emit a failure event at the 24h boundary. This is the non-negotiable: if you only fire on success, every experiment looks like it worked.

Roll raw event into a metric tree: Signups (vanity) → activation_rate (the decision metric) → retention → north-star. Each level is caused by the one below it, so the number you act on sits on the causal path.
Pre-commit the invalidation threshold: activation_rate < 25% kills v2 — written BEFORE data arrives. A threshold set after you see the result is a rationalization.
The fire-rate guard: If the event fires for < 95% of eligible users, the pipeline is dropping signal — decide NOTHING until it's fixed. This is the repair path from the diagram.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

instrumentation.title: The instrumentation feedback loop — and where signal dies
instrumentation.subtitle: User action → event fires → pipeline → metric tree → decision. The silent-drop failure path (event never emitted / lost in the pipe) makes the dashboard lie; the repair path is a fire-rate check that catches the gap before you trust the number.

legend.label: metric tree → the decision it feeds

storyboard.say: It starts with a user doing the thing that matters — the action on the causal path to retention, the moment worth measuring.
That action is supposed to fire one instrumented event — the single wire connecting a shipped feature to a real decision.
The event ships through the pipeline, gets aggregated into your metric tree, and rolls up toward the north-star number.
That tree informs the decision — ship, kill, double down — as long as every event on the path actually arrived.
But here's where signal dies: a guard skips the emit, the event is never fired, and it drops silently with no error.
The dropped event undercounts the tree — the dashboard stays green while you false-kill the feature users never reached.
The repair is a fire-rate check: verify the event actually fires at expected volume before you trust the number.
The invariant: pick the invalidating number and its threshold before the data arrives, or it will rationalize any result.

## Instrumentation Spec
event: user_activated
  props: { user_id, segment, ts, first_project_created: bool, teammate_invited: bool }
  fires_when: first_project_created == true AND teammate_invited == true, within 24h of signup
  fires_on_drop: emit user_activation_failed{user_id, last_step} at the 24h boundary

## Metric Tree (raw event -> north-star)
  signups                     (top of funnel, vanity)
   └─ activation_rate = activated / signups        <- THE decision metric
       └─ week1_retention (activated cohort)
           └─ NSM: weekly_active_teams

## Invalidation Threshold (pre-committed, before launch)
  activation_rate < 25% for the new-onboarding segment  ->  KILL v2, revert to v1
  fire-rate check: user_activated emitted for < 95% of eligible users -> instrumentation is broken, DECIDE NOTHING

steps.label: Name the event + its schema
steps.note: user_activated with typed props. 'we track activation' is a wish; a schema with user_id, segment, and ts is instrumentation a reviewer can inspect.

steps.label: Define the aha-moment precisely
steps.note: Activation is the AND of the two actions that predict retention — chosen from customer discovery, not from what was easy to log.

steps.label: Instrument the DROP, not just the win
steps.note: Emit a failure event at the 24h boundary. This is the non-negotiable: if you only fire on success, every experiment looks like it worked.

steps.label: Roll raw event into a metric tree
steps.note: Signups (vanity) → activation_rate (the decision metric) → retention → north-star. Each level is caused by the one below it, so the number you act on sits on the causal path.

steps.label: Pre-commit the invalidation threshold
steps.note: activation_rate < 25% kills v2 — written BEFORE data arrives. A threshold set after you see the result is a rationalization.

steps.label: The fire-rate guard
steps.note: If the event fires for < 95% of eligible users, the pipeline is dropping signal — decide NOTHING until it's fixed. This is the repair path from the diagram.

instrumentation.text: The senior move nobody tells you: write the invalidation threshold and the fire-rate check into the packet BEFORE the feature ships. Instrumentation added after launch always gets tuned — consciously or not — until the data agrees with the team that shipped it. instrumentation.question: A reviewer asks for the exact evidence that your instrumentation is trustworthy, not just a happy-path answer. Which response actually proves it?
options: "The dashboard shows signups and clicks are both up since launch."

"Activation is defined as an event with a schema, it fires on both the aha-moment and the 24h drop-off, the fire-rate is 96% of eligible users, and activation_rate came in under the 25% threshold we set before launch — so we killed v2."
"We added analytics to the new onboarding flow and the numbers look good."
"Retention will probably improve because the new flow feels smoother."
instrumentation.explanation: Only option 2 points to the four things a reviewer can inspect: a real event schema, an event that records the DROP (not just success), a verified fire-rate proving the pipeline isn't silently under-counting, and a pre-committed threshold that produced an actual kill. The others are vanity metrics (1), an unverified claim (3), and a feeling (4) — none can be falsified.

feedback-intake.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'gathered feedback' if your intake only collected quotes that agree with the thing you already wanted to build. Curated praise is not evidence — it is a highlight reel. Feedback intake that can only say 'yes' is theater; the invariant is that the experiment must be able to invalidate the bet.

feedback-intake.text: Two teams ship the same feature. One read 40 support tickets, cherry-picked the five that loved the idea, and built for a quarter — activation never moved. The other ran one 20-user experiment, watched retention flatline in week two, and killed the bet on a Tuesday. Same feedback, opposite outcomes: one team framed intake to confirm, the other framed it to invalidate.

Feedback Intake sits in the production-pressure phase of Product Execution: it is the joint where market evidence becomes a scoped engineering decision. Done right it feeds the PRD, the metric tree, and the launch; done as a note, it lets a confident guess masquerade as customer demand.

feedback-intake.prompt: 'I talked to ten customers and they all said they wanted this.' Before you fund the build — what is wrong with that as feedback intake? Answer before reading on.
feedback-intake.reveal: It is confirmation wearing a lab coat. 'They wanted it' is a stated preference, not a measured behavior, and ten hand-picked yeses can't fail — so they prove nothing. Real intake names the assumption ('users will complete setup if we remove step 3'), attaches an activation metric ('setup-completion rate'), and sets an invalidation threshold ('if it doesn't beat 42% we don't ship'). The number can go the wrong way. That risk of being wrong is the whole value.

feedback-intake.code:
# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Context
New signups reach the empty dashboard and stall. Sales blames onboarding; support has 38 tickets.

## Assumption (falsifiable)
Users fail to activate because setup has too many steps — a guided wizard will lift day-1 activation.

## Experiment
Concierge test: 20 new signups from the discovery interview pool. 10 get the wizard prototype, 10 get current setup. Run 2 weeks.

## Metric tree
- North star: week-2 retention
  - Activation metric: % completing setup on day 1  (current baseline 34%)
  - Guardrail: support tickets per signup (must not rise)

## Invalidation threshold
If wizard cohort day-1 activation does NOT beat 42% (baseline + 8pt), OR week-2 retention is flat, the assumption is invalidated — do not build.

## Chosen vs rejected
- Chosen: wizard prototype behind a flag for 20 users (cheap, reversible)
- Rejected: build the full wizard for all users now (expensive, one-way door)
- Reversal condition: below threshold → kill wizard, re-frame the activation problem

## Expected failure
Activation rises but retention stays flat — setup was never the real churn cause.

## Reviewer objection
"Show me the result that would have STOPPED this build." → the 42% / flat-retention threshold above.

## Repair notes
If activation < 42%: assumption wrong at the step-count layer → route back to discovery, not to a bigger wizard.

## Capstone connection
This packet feeds the capstone PRD's success metrics and the launch's invalidation gate.
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
Context — the feedback, not the fix: 38 tickets and a sales complaint are signal. Naming them keeps intake honest: this is where the bet came from, and it is not yet a decision.
The falsifiable assumption: 'Too many steps → wizard lifts activation' can be wrong. If your assumption cannot be false, you have a wish, not a bet.
The smallest experiment: A concierge test on 20 users — not a full build. The experiment must be cheap enough to run before you commit engineering.
The metric tree: Activation reads the immediate result; retention is the north star; a guardrail catches a metric you'd otherwise game. Feedback with no metric can't be read.
The invalidation threshold: 42% or flat retention → stop. This line is the deliverable — it is the number that can kill your favorite feature.
Chosen, rejected, reversal: Flagged prototype (two-way door) over full build (one-way door). The reversal condition is what makes this a decision, not a hope.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

storyboard.say: Everything starts with raw support feedback — noisy, muted, external. It is evidence, not yet a decision. The first move is to distill it.
Distilling feedback into a named assumption is the fork in the road: state the belief the feature depends on, out loud.
The dashed shortcut is the trap: skip the test and feedback becomes a curated guess — five cherry-picked tickets dressed as customer demand.
The honest path makes the assumption falsifiable: design the smallest experiment that could actually prove it wrong.
The experiment instruments a metric tree — activation, retention — so the result is measured, not narrated.
Read the metric against the invalidation threshold you set up front. This is the joint where the intake earns the right to say no.
Below the bar, route back to repair: rewrite the assumption instead of shipping. That is how one team killed the bet on a Tuesday.
Clear the bar and it becomes a decision memo — market evidence turned into a scoped, defensible engineering commitment.
