# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Context
New signups reach the empty dashboard and stall. Sales blames onboarding; support has 38 tickets.

## Assumption (falsifiable)
Users fail to activate because setup has too many steps — a guided wizard will lift day-1 activation.

## Experiment
Concierge test: 20 new signups from the discovery interview pool. 10 get the wizard prototype, 10 get current setup. Run 2 weeks.

## Metric tree
- North star: week-2 retention
  - Activation metric: % completing setup on day 1  (current baseline 34%)
  - Guardrail: support tickets per signup (must not rise)

## Invalidation threshold
If wizard cohort day-1 activation does NOT beat 42% (baseline + 8pt), OR week-2 retention is flat, the assumption is invalidated — do not build.

## Chosen vs rejected
- Chosen: wizard prototype behind a flag for 20 users (cheap, reversible)
- Rejected: build the full wizard for all users now (expensive, one-way door)
- Reversal condition: below threshold → kill wizard, re-frame the activation problem

## Expected failure
Activation rises but retention stays flat — setup was never the real churn cause.

## Reviewer objection
"Show me the result that would have STOPPED this build." → the 42% / flat-retention threshold above.

## Repair notes
If activation < 42%: assumption wrong at the step-count layer → route back to discovery, not to a bigger wizard.

## Capstone connection
This packet feeds the capstone PRD's success metrics and the launch's invalidation gate.

steps.label: Context — the feedback, not the fix
steps.note: 38 tickets and a sales complaint are signal. Naming them keeps intake honest: this is where the bet came from, and it is not yet a decision.

steps.label: The falsifiable assumption
steps.note: 'Too many steps → wizard lifts activation' can be wrong. If your assumption cannot be false, you have a wish, not a bet.

steps.label: The smallest experiment
steps.note: A concierge test on 20 users — not a full build. The experiment must be cheap enough to run before you commit engineering.

steps.label: The metric tree
steps.note: Activation reads the immediate result; retention is the north star; a guardrail catches a metric you'd otherwise game. Feedback with no metric can't be read.

steps.label: The invalidation threshold
steps.note: 42% or flat retention → stop. This line is the deliverable — it is the number that can kill your favorite feature.

steps.label: Chosen, rejected, reversal
steps.note: Flagged prototype (two-way door) over full build (one-way door). The reversal condition is what makes this a decision, not a hope.

feedback-intake.text: The senior tell, grounded in DORA's measurement-driven approach to delivery: teams that decide from a metric tend to move faster and reverse cheaper than teams that decide from the loudest quote. State the number that would change your mind BEFORE you run the experiment — a threshold written after the result is a story, not a decision.

prioritization.text: Sprint planning, eight tickets, one team, and the loudest voice in the room wants the feature that demos well to the board. The PM asks one question — "which of these actually moves activation, and how do we know?" — and the roadmap that felt obvious ten seconds ago goes quiet.

Every product decision is a bet placed with finite engineering time against uncertain market evidence. Prioritization is the artifact that converts "everyone wants their thing first" into one ranked, evidence-backed order — the packet section your capstone discovery, PRD, and experiment plan all inherit.

prioritization.prompt: "This feature is high-impact, so it goes first." Before you defend that ordering — what is missing from it as a prioritization? Answer before reading on.
prioritization.reveal: Impact alone is one axis of a multi-axis bet. A high-impact feature you are 20% confident in, that touches 4% of users, and costs a quarter, loses to a medium-impact fix you are 90% confident in, that touches everyone, and ships in a week. Prioritization is impact ÷ effort, weighted by reach and by confidence — and confidence is the axis amateurs skip, because it is the one that demands customer evidence instead of opinion.

steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
One model, every row: Same four axes for the exec's pet feature and the unglamorous fix. A shared scale is what lets you compare a demo darling to a search bug at all.
The winner, and why it wins: High reach (8000), real impact (2.0), high confidence (0.9) backed by an activation cohort — cheap effort. Score isn't a feeling; it's arithmetic on evidence.
The evidence-free bet exposed: AI import scores 67 because confidence is 0.2 — '0 interviews, exec excitement only'. The model doesn't ban HiPPO features; it prices their missing evidence.
Cheap + certain beats flashy + unsure: The stale-index fix ties the top score at effort 1. An unglamorous, fully-evidenced fix routinely out-ranks the thing that demos well.
Name the rejected option out loud: Deferring AI import in writing, with the reason, is the difference between a decision and a shrug. The rejected bet is part of the artifact.
The invalidation threshold: A concrete metric ('< 5 pt activation lift') that flips the ranking. Without it, prioritization is a one-way opinion; with it, it's a reversible, testable bet.

prioritization.subtitle: Customer evidence feeds confidence; the four axes feed one score; the score feeds a ranked order gated by an invalidation threshold. Opinion is deliberately kept OUT of the confidence input.

storyboard.say: Eight tickets, one team, and the loudest voice wants the board demo. The real entry point isn't opinion — it's customer evidence.
Evidence grounds confidence: how sure we are must trace to an actual customer signal, not a hunch.
Here's the guardrail: opinion and the HiPPO may inform debate, but they must NOT set confidence directly.
Every candidate gets scored on the same four axes — reach, impact, confidence, and effort — no exceptions.
The formula combines them: reach times impact times confidence, divided by effort, yields one comparable score.
Score orders the candidates into one ranked roadmap — the artifact your PRD and experiment plan inherit.
One last gate: an invalidation threshold can reverse the rank if the evidence stops holding up.

| Bet                     | Reach | Impact | Conf | Effort | Score | Evidence for confidence            |
|-------------------------|-------|--------|------|--------|-------|------------------------------------|
| Onboarding checklist    | 8000  | 2.0    | 0.9  | 2      | 7200  | activation cohort: 41% drop at step 2 |
| AI import (board demo)  | 900   | 3.0    | 0.2  | 8      |  67   | 0 interviews; exec excitement only |
| Fix stale search index  | 8000  | 1.0    | 0.9  | 1      | 7200  | 12/15 interviews named stale results |

prioritization.text: The senior tell: they prioritize the confidence axis by going and getting evidence, not by arguing harder. When a PM says 'confidence is 0.2 because we've talked to nobody', that is not weakness — it is the cheapest next action (five interviews) surfacing itself. NIST AI RMF's MEASURE function calls for pairing performance assessment with "associated measures of uncertainty" and documenting them, so risk can be managed; a blank confidence column is unmeasured, undocumented uncertainty. (Note: "making uncertainty explicit" is a paraphrase; NIST's exact phrasing is "associated measures of uncertainty," and it never uses the phrase "confidence column.")

prioritization.question: Two bets tie on reach and impact. Bet A is 90% confident (backed by an activation cohort) and costs 2 weeks. Bet B is 30% confident (an exec's hunch) and costs 8 weeks. What does a defensible prioritization do?
options: Build Bet B first — the exec sponsors it and it demos well.

Rank Bet A above Bet B: higher confidence from real evidence and lower effort both raise its expected value per unit of effort — and log a cheap experiment to raise B's confidence before it competes again.
Build them in parallel so nobody is unhappy.
Flip a coin — the scores are basically equal.
prioritization.explanation: Prioritization is expected value per unit of effort. A tie on reach and impact is broken by confidence and effort: A is more evidenced (0.9 vs 0.3) and cheaper (2 vs 8 weeks), so it ranks higher on both terms. B is not banned — its problem is missing evidence, so the right move is a cheap experiment to earn a real confidence number before it re-competes. Sponsorship (1) and coin-flips (3, 4) discard the evidence the model exists to weigh.

prioritization.intro: Prove your Prioritization holds — no vibes:
items: Every candidate is scored on the SAME axes (reach, impact, confidence, effort). If one item is scored differently than the rest, the ranking is not comparable — fix it.

Every confidence number cites a source: an interview count, an activation/retention cohort, or an experiment result. A confidence with no evidence line is an opinion — mark it 'unevidenced' and treat that as its own backlog item.
Your #1 wins on arithmetic a skeptic could re-derive from your table, not on who sponsors it.
The rejected bet is named in writing with the reason it lost — a decision names what it did NOT do.
An invalidation threshold exists: a concrete metric result that would reverse the ranking, so the bet is reversible instead of a one-way opinion.

roadmap-strategy.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a roadmap strategy if the packet is a prioritized feature list. A roadmap ordered by opinion is a wish list. The strategy is the decision rule: which market evidence would move each bet up, down, or off the board — and the threshold that flips it.

roadmap-strategy.text: The quarter's roadmap is locked, six engineers are three sprints deep on the flagship feature, and in the customer call the words land like a verdict: "we would never turn this on." Nobody had written down the assumption that feature was betting the quarter on, so nobody knew it had just been invalidated.

This lesson sits in the production-pressure phase, where problem framing, discovery, PRDs, and metric trees converge into what you actually commit to build. Roadmap Strategy is the artifact that connects market evidence to scoped engineering decisions — the reviewable link between "customers said this" and "so we build that, and stop building the other thing."

roadmap-strategy.prompt: "Q3 roadmap: 1) Collaboration mode, 2) SSO, 3) Mobile app." Before you argue the priority order — what is missing that makes this not a strategy? Answer before reading on.
roadmap-strategy.reveal: There is no way for it to be wrong. A real roadmap strategy carries, for each bet, the assumption it depends on and the evidence that would kill it: "Collaboration mode assumes teams share workspaces daily; if activation on the shared-workspace event stays under 15% in a 40-user pilot, we cut it." A ranked feature list is a set of guesses in confidence order; a strategy is a set of falsifiable bets with invalidation thresholds. The list feels like a decision precisely because it hides the assumptions it never tested.

# Roadmap Decision Packet - Collaboration Mode

## Context
- Segment: 5-15 person product teams already paying for the solo plan
- Roadmap bet: build real-time collaboration mode this quarter (6 eng, 2 sprints)

## Assumptions (the bet rides on these)
- A1: solo users share a workspace with teammates >= 3x/week
- A2: shared-workspace teams retain better than solo (the upsell thesis)

## Selected approach
- Concierge experiment first: 12 discovery interviews + a fake-door
  "Invite your team" button, 40-user pilot, measured 2 weeks

## Rejected approach
- Build the full real-time engine first, then measure adoption
  (2 sprints sunk before any market signal - reversal gets expensive)

## Metric tree
- Activation: % of pilot users who fire share_workspace >= 1x  (leading)
- Retention: week-2 retention of sharers vs solo               (thesis)

## Invalidation threshold
- CUT if share_workspace activation < 15% OR sharer W2 retention
  is not > solo retention by >= 8 pts. Reversal is automatic, not a debate.

## Expected failure
- Vanity read: high fake-door clicks (curiosity) but < 15% real activation

## Reviewer objection / repair / capstone below
- (filled in the callout, quiz, and transfer sections)
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
Name the segment, not "users": "5-15 person teams on the solo plan" is a segment you can recruit and measure. "Our users" is not a segment; it is everyone, which is no one.
Surface the assumption the bet rides on: A1 and A2 are the load-bearing beliefs. If you cannot write the assumption, you cannot invalidate it — and an un-invalidatable bet is faith, not strategy.

Cheapest invalidating experiment first: Concierge + fake-door buys the same signal as the full build for a fraction of the cost. The rule mirrors diagnosis: run the cheapest test that can return "no" first.
Rejected approach, on the record: Building first, measuring later, makes reversal cost two sprints. Naming the rejected path is what makes the choice defensible in review.
Metric tree: leading + thesis: Activation is the leading signal (do they even try it); retention is the upsell thesis (does it make them stickier). One without the other is half a decision.
The invalidation threshold is a number: "< 15% activation OR not +8pts retention -> CUT." A threshold you set before the data arrives is what stops conviction from re-interpreting a miss as a win.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

# Writing the decision packet, one section at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real product bet you are tempted to build and convert it into a Roadmap Strategy decision: write customer_experiment_and_metric_decision_packet.md that names the market segment, the assumption you must invalidate, the cheapest experiment that could kill the bet, the activation/retention metric that would confirm it, and the invalidation threshold that reverses the roadmap.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only pack_roadmap at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Every roadmap bet names a specific, recruitable market segment — not "our users".
# 2. Every bet has a written assumption, and you can state the experiment result that would invalidate it.
# 3. The chosen experiment is the cheapest thing that can return "no" — it does not require the full build to run.
# 4. The metric tree has both a leading activation metric and a thesis retention metric, with a numeric invalidation threshold set BEFORE the data arrives.
# 5. The rejected approach and the reversal condition are on the record — a reviewer can see what you did not choose and what would flip the decision.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

BETS = [
    ("collab-mode", 0.35, 90.0, 6),
    ("sso", 0.80, 40.0, 4),
    ("onboard-fix", 0.70, 50.0, 3),
    ("usage-billing", 0.50, 70.0, 5),
]
CAPACITY = 12


def ev_per_week(bet):
    name, p, payoff, wks = bet
    return p * payoff / wks


def pack_roadmap(bets, capacity):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

for bet in sorted(BETS, key=ev_per_week, reverse=True):
    name, p, payoff, wks = bet
    print(f"{name}: EV {p * payoff:.1f} over {wks} wks = {ev_per_week(bet):.1f}/wk")
chosen, used, ev = pack_roadmap(BETS, CAPACITY)
print(f"packed ({used}/{CAPACITY} wks): {', '.join(chosen)}")
print(f"portfolio EV: {ev:.1f}")
out = [b[0] for b in BETS if b[0] not in chosen]
print(f"excluded: {out[0]} -> resurrection: 10 interviews, >=6 unprompted lifts p to 0.6")

roadmap-strategy.title: The roadmap decision loop — evidence in, scoped build out
roadmap-strategy.subtitle: A candidate bet flows through discovery, the cheapest invalidating experiment, and a metric tree gate. The invalidation threshold is the decision node: below it the bet is cut and the roadmap re-ranks; above it, it becomes a scoped build. The vision-deck path is deliberately out — conviction does not enter the loop.

nodes.label: Invalidation threshold
nodes.description: the number that reverses the bet

legend.label: the scoped build the loop exists to earn

storyboard.say: Every roadmap bet starts here: a real market segment. That segment scopes the one key assumption the whole feature is riding on.
Notice what does NOT feed the assumption: the vision deck. Conviction is deliberately out of the loop — it must not decide the bet.
From the assumption we design the cheapest experiment that could invalidate it — not the fanciest, the fastest to prove us wrong.
The experiment produces a signal, which flows into the metric tree gate — an activation or retention number, not an opinion.
That metric is compared against the invalidation threshold — the numeric line, written down in advance, that reverses the decision.
Fall below the threshold and the bet is cut — the roadmap re-ranks and six engineers do not spend three sprints on a dead feature.
Clear the threshold and only then does it become a scoped build — the reviewable link from what customers said to what we commit.
The invariant: every bet names its segment, assumption, experiment, metric, and threshold — so evidence, not conviction, can always kill it.

steps.note: "5-15 person teams on the solo plan" is a segment you can recruit and measure. "Our users" is not a segment; it is everyone, which is no one.

steps.label: Surface the assumption the bet rides on
steps.note: A1 and A2 are the load-bearing beliefs. If you cannot write the assumption, you cannot invalidate it — and an un-invalidatable bet is faith, not strategy.

steps.label: Cheapest invalidating experiment first
steps.note: Concierge + fake-door buys the same signal as the full build for a fraction of the cost. The rule mirrors diagnosis: run the cheapest test that can return "no" first.

steps.label: Rejected approach, on the record
steps.note: Building first, measuring later, makes reversal cost two sprints. Naming the rejected path is what makes the choice defensible in review.

steps.label: Metric tree: leading + thesis
steps.note: Activation is the leading signal (do they even try it); retention is the upsell thesis (does it make them stickier). One without the other is half a decision.

steps.label: The invalidation threshold is a number
steps.note: "< 15% activation OR not +8pts retention -> CUT." A threshold you set before the data arrives is what stops conviction from re-interpreting a miss as a win.

roadmap-strategy.caption: A roadmap you can only be right about is a wish list. A roadmap that names the number that would make you wrong is a strategy.

roadmap-strategy.text: The senior product tell: decisions are traceable to evidence. NIST AI RMF supports the traceability half directly ("measurement provides a traceable basis to inform management decisions"); the "stated reversal condition" is a reasonable extension of MANAGE 2.4's deactivation mechanisms but NIST does not use the term "reversal condition," and ABET does not speak to this at all. A staff PM does not defend a bet by restating the vision; they point to the invalidation threshold and say "here is the number that would make me cut my own feature." A roadmap whose bets can only be confirmed, never killed, is a feedback loop with the feedback removed.

roadmap-strategy.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence that this roadmap bet is not just a happy-path answer." Which packet earns the pass?
options: One that ranks the quarter's features by projected revenue and shows a polished vision deck.
One that names the segment, the assumption, the cheapest invalidating experiment, an activation+retention metric tree, and a numeric invalidation threshold that would cut the bet.
One where every proposed feature has a detailed PRD and design mockup.
One with strong customer quotes praising the idea from the discovery calls.
roadmap-strategy.explanation: The reviewer is testing for falsifiability and evidence traceability, not polish. Only option 2 makes the bet killable: it ties the decision to an experiment that can return "no" and a threshold that reverses the roadmap. Revenue ranking (1) and PRDs (3) presume the bet is already right; cherry-picked praise quotes (4) are exactly the happy-path selection the reviewer is hunting for.

roadmap-strategy.intro: Prove the packet is a strategy, not a wish list:
items: Every roadmap bet names a specific, recruitable market segment — not "our users".
Every bet has a written assumption, and you can state the experiment result that would invalidate it.
The chosen experiment is the cheapest thing that can return "no" — it does not require the full build to run.
The metric tree has both a leading activation metric and a thesis retention metric, with a numeric invalidation threshold set BEFORE the data arrives.
The rejected approach and the reversal condition are on the record — a reviewer can see what you did not choose and what would flip the decision.

go-to-market.text: The deck says 'huge market, obvious need, launch in six weeks.' A staff PM asks one question — 'which segment, and what would have to be true for them to actually adopt?' — and the room realizes it built a roadmap on a market it never tested. The build was real. The customer was a guess.

Going to market is the moment product evidence either exists or gets faked. This lesson turns 'we think people want this' into a scoped experiment, an activation metric, and a pre-committed invalidation threshold — the feedback loop that connects market reality to what engineering actually builds next.

go-to-market.prompt: "Users love the demo — let's launch to everyone." Before you debate the launch, what is wrong with that as go-to-market evidence? Answer before reading on.
go-to-market.reveal: "Love the demo" measures enthusiasm, not adoption — and 'everyone' is not a segment. Demo delight is a notorious false positive: people compliment what they will never use. The real signal is retention inside one named segment (do week-2 users come back?) against a threshold you set before launch. Launching to 'everyone' on a demo cheer means you can never tell which market actually pulled — you invalidate nothing and learn nothing.

# Go-To-Market Decision Packet

## Segment
- Beachhead: solo Shopify sellers doing $5k-$20k/mo (not 'SMBs')
- Discovery signal: 9/12 interviews named 'abandoned-cart follow-up' unprompted

## Riskiest assumption
- They will connect their store on day 1 (integration friction kills adoption)

## Experiment
- Test: concierge MVP — 30 sellers, manual setup offered, self-serve optional
- Activation metric: % who connect store AND send 1 campaign within 48h
- Retention metric: % of activated sellers who return in week 2
- Invalidation threshold (pre-set): activation < 40% OR week-2 retention < 25% -> do NOT build self-serve

## Rejected option
- Broad paid-ads launch to 'all e-commerce' — no segment, cannot attribute pull

## Reviewer objection + repair
- Objection: 'demo love' logged as signal -> repair: only count sent campaigns, not sign-ups
- Capstone: this packet + its metric tree feeds the product capstone's launch + feedback report
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
One named segment: 'Solo Shopify sellers at $5k-$20k/mo' is a beachhead. 'SMBs' is a wish. The narrower the segment, the sharper the signal.
Discovery signal, quantified: 9 of 12 interviews naming the pain UNPROMPTED is customer discovery evidence — not 'people seemed interested'.
The riskiest assumption: Not every assumption — the ONE whose failure sinks the launch. Integration friction, not feature count, is what actually kills adoption here.
Activation, tied to behavior: Activation = connect store AND send a campaign. Two real actions, not a sign-up. A metric that measures intent instead of behavior lies to you.
Retention, the honest signal: Week-2 return separates a demo cheer from a product. Adoption without retention is a launch that quietly churns.
The invalidation threshold: Written BEFORE data: activation < 40% OR retention < 25% stops the build. This single line is what makes it an experiment, not an announcement.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

A peer reads it and can tell you the exact number at which you would NOT ship.

# Writing the decision packet, one line at a time
#
# Mission: Take one product-launch decision you actually face (or a realistic one) and write the Go-To-Market packet: the market segment you are serving, the riskiest assumption, the one experiment that would invalidate it, the activation metric that proves adoption, and the invalidation threshold that would stop the build. Not a plan — a decision packet a reviewer can sign.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only channel_economics at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your segment aloud. If it is a category ('SMBs', 'e-commerce'), narrow it to one beachhead you could list interviewees from.
# 2. Point to the invalidation threshold and confirm it was written BEFORE any data. If you can't say the number that would stop the launch, you have no experiment.
# 3. Check the activation metric measures a real action (connected, sent, returned), not intent (signed up, clicked, said yes).
# 4. Confirm a retention metric exists — adoption without week-2 return is a demo cheer, not a product.
# 5. Hand the packet to a peer and ask them to state the number at which you would NOT ship. If they can't find it, it isn't in there.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

CHANNELS = [
    ("paid-search", 4000.0, 210, 50),
    ("content-seo", 1500.0, 60, 12),
    ("partner-apps", 2400.0, 130, 40),
]
MARGIN = 32.0
BAR = 3.0


def channel_economics(channel, margin):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

rows = []
for ch in CHANNELS:
    name, spend, signups, activated = ch
    cac, payback = channel_economics(ch, MARGIN)
    act_rate = activated / signups * 100
    rows.append((payback, name, cac, act_rate))
    print(f"{name}: CAC ${cac:.0f}/activated ({act_rate:.0f}% activation), payback {payback:.1f} mo")
rows.sort()
best = rows[0]
print(f"best channel: {best[1]} at {best[0]:.1f} mo")
for payback, name, cac, _ in rows:
    verdict = "SCALE" if payback <= BAR * 0.7 else ("KEEP" if payback <= BAR else "FAILS BAR - do not scale")
    print(f"{name}: {verdict}")

best channel: partner-apps at 1.9 mo
partner-apps: SCALE

storyboard.say: The deck says huge market, launch in six weeks. Start where evidence has to start: customer discovery, narrowing to one real market segment.
One segment surfaces its riskiest assumption: the single thing that, if false, sinks the entire launch.
That assumption becomes a test. The experiment turns 'we think people want this' into something reality can answer.
The experiment measures activation and retention. This is the store of evidence the launch decision will actually stand on.
Those metrics are compared against an invalidation threshold written before the data. A launch that cannot fail was never a test.
On pass, the threshold greenlights a scoped build and ship. Evidence, not the deck, unlocks engineering.
On fail, it routes straight back to discovery. The loop closes instead of committing to a market it never tested.
Pricing and full launch stay out until the loop closes. They must not jump ahead of the build the evidence earned.

pricing-packaging.text: The product is built, the launch is Monday, and someone finally asks "so what do we charge?" — the room throws out $9, $29, $99, everyone nods, and a number nobody can defend becomes the number that decides whether the company lives.

Pricing and packaging is the feedback loop where market evidence meets the build: the same product at the wrong price gates the wrong segment, starves activation, and hides real demand. This is the Pricing & Packaging section of the decision packet you carry through the course — the artifact that turns "what feels fair" into a decision with a threshold that can be proven wrong.

pricing-packaging.prompt: "Competitors charge $29/mo, so we'll charge $24 to undercut them." Before you debate the number — what is wrong with that as a pricing decision? Answer before reading on.
pricing-packaging.reveal: It prices the competitor, not your customer. Undercutting assumes you serve the same segment, deliver the same value metric, and win on price — three unproven leaps. It also anchors you below your own willingness-to-pay evidence: if your discovery interviews say a design agency would pay $80/seat to kill a workflow, $24 leaves 3x on the table and signals "cheap tool" to the exact buyer you want. Price is a claim about who you serve and what value you meter — not a reaction to a rival's page.

pricing-packaging.code:
## Pricing & Packaging
- Segment: 5-15 person design agencies (buyer = studio lead)
- Value metric: active editor seats (scales with the pain, not usage spikes)
- Packaging:
  - Solo   $19/seat/mo  -> gates: 1 brand kit,  no SSO
  - Studio $49/seat/mo  -> gates: unlimited kits, shared library, SSO
  - Scale  custom       -> gates: audit log, SLA, procurement
- WTP evidence: 7/9 discovery interviews said a lost brand-kit costs a re-pitch (~$4k); competitor Frontify anchors at $99/seat
- Assumption: agencies pay per-seat, not per-project (per-project would invert the metric)
- Selected: land on Studio $49, expand seats; Solo is the trial magnet
- Rejected: flat $99/studio (kills expansion revenue; ignores seat = value metric)
- Invalidation threshold: kill Studio price if <8% of Solo trials upgrade within 30 days OR median deal < 3 seats
- Verification: 30-day trial cohort, conversion + seats-per-account instrumented
- Reviewer objection: "$49 is an anchor, not evidence" -> answered by the re-pitch cost + Frontify anchor above
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
Name the segment first: Not "SMBs" — a specific buyer (5-15 person agencies, studio lead signs). Price serves a segment; a segment you cannot name cannot be priced.
Pick the value metric: The unit that scales with the customer's value, not your cost. Seats track the pain here; metering per-render would punish the heaviest, happiest users.
Package by what each tier GATES: Tiers are not price rows — they are value fences. SSO and shared library are the wedge that moves a studio from Solo to Studio.
Attach willingness-to-pay evidence: The re-pitch cost quantifies pain; the Frontify anchor bounds the ceiling. Evidence bands the number — this is what separates a price from a guess.
State the pricing assumption: "Agencies pay per-seat not per-project." If this is false, the whole value metric inverts. Naming it makes it testable.
Selected vs rejected, with the reason: Flat $99/studio is the tempting simple option — rejected because it destroys seat-expansion revenue and ignores the value metric.
The invalidation threshold — the whole point: A concrete number that would prove the price wrong: <8% trial-to-paid OR median deal <3 seats. Past it, the price is falsified, not defended.
Verification + pre-answered objection: Instrument conversion and seats-per-account so the threshold can actually fire; pre-empt "$49 is an anchor" with the evidence line above.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

# Writing the Pricing & Packaging section, one line at a time
#
# Mission: Take one real product you could charge for and produce the Pricing & Packaging section of customer_experiment_and_metric_decision_packet.md: the packaging structure (what tiers, what gates each tier), one price point per tier, the willingness-to-pay evidence behind it, and the single invalidation threshold that would prove the price wrong.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only revenue_at at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Name the segment for each tier out loud. If the answer is "everyone" or "SMBs," you have not segmented — a price you cannot aim cannot be defended.
# 2. Point to the value metric and say why it scales with the customer's value, not your cost. If billing goes up when their success does NOT, the metric is wrong.
# 3. For each price, show at least one piece of willingness-to-pay evidence (interview quote, competitor anchor, or Van Westendorp band). A price with only "it feels right" is a guess.
# 4. State the one invalidation threshold as a number a dashboard could show (e.g. <8% trial-to-paid in 30 days). If nothing could ever prove the price wrong, it is not a decision.
# 5. Confirm the rejected packaging option is written down with the reason it lost — so the choice is defensible, not just asserted.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

WTP = [19, 19, 24, 29, 29, 29, 34, 39, 39, 39,
       44, 49, 49, 49, 54, 59, 59, 64, 79, 99]
CANDIDATES = [19, 29, 39, 49, 59]
UNDERCUT = 24


def revenue_at(price, wtp):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

best = None
for p in CANDIDATES:
    buyers, rev = revenue_at(p, WTP)
    print(f"${p}: {buyers}/20 buy -> ${rev} per 20 prospects")
    if best is None or rev > best[1]:
        best = (p, rev)
print(f"revenue peak: ${best[0]} (${best[1]})")
ub, ur = revenue_at(UNDERCUT, WTP)
print(f"undercut instinct ${UNDERCUT}: {ub}/20 buy -> ${ur} (donates ${best[1] - ur})")
print("kill-number: trial->paid at the peak price must be >=8% or drop a tier and re-read")

pricing-packaging.subtitle: Segment and value metric feed the packaging tiers; willingness-to-pay evidence sets the band; the live experiment feeds back an invalidation threshold. storyboard.say: It's launch week and someone asks what to charge. The temptation is a round-number guess — but that guess must NOT set the price.
Start instead with a named market segment. Who exactly is this for? That segment is what packaging targets.
Pick the value metric you meter — seats, events, GMV — and let it feed the same packaging tiers.
Segment and metric together shape the tiers, and the tiers set the actual price point.
Willingness-to-pay evidence bands the number — it constrains the range so the price isn't invented.
Ship that price to one segment as a live test, then measure it against an invalidation threshold — its kill-number.
The repair path: a miss routes back to re-package or re-segment — never to a random discount.
The invariant: every price carries a threshold that could prove it wrong. A price with no kill-number is a guess wearing a decimal point.

pricing-packaging.text: The tell that separates a founder from a discounter: the value metric is chosen so the customer's bill grows only when their success grows. If your metric bills people for using the product more (seats they had to add, events they had to process), expansion is automatic and churn is aligned. If it bills them for pain (per-seat when value is per-project), you've built a meter that punishes your happiest customers — and you'll blame "the market" when they leave. Grounded in the NIST AI RMF MEASURE discipline of assessing and documenting metric appropriateness and effectiveness: a metric you can't tie to measured value is a metric you can't govern. (This is an inference in the spirit of MEASURE; NIST does not state the aphorism verbatim.)

pricing-packaging.question: A reviewer says: "Show me the exact evidence that this $49 price isn't just a happy-path guess." Which response actually proves the pricing decision?
options: "$49 sits nicely between our $19 and $99 tiers, so it's balanced."
"7 of 9 discovery interviews put the cost of a lost brand kit at ~$4k, a competitor anchors at $99/seat, and we'll kill the $49 tier if fewer than 8% of trials convert in 30 days."
"Our competitors charge around that, so it's market rate."
"It's a round, memorable number that customers respond to well."
pricing-packaging.explanation: Only option 2 points to willingness-to-pay evidence (the $4k re-pitch pain and the $99 competitor anchor that band the price) AND an invalidation threshold (kill if <8% convert in 30 days) that lets a live experiment prove the price wrong. The others reason from position within your own tiers (1), a competitor (3), or aesthetics (4) — none of which is evidence a reviewer, or the market, can falsify.

launch-readiness.text: The team spent nine weeks building the feature everyone loved in the hallway. It shipped to silence: activation flat, retention untouched, the loudest fans never came back. Nobody had written down, in advance, the number that would have said 'stop.'

Launch readiness is the last gate before you spend real engineering on a bet: it converts 'customers seem excited' into one experiment with a metric it must move and a threshold that could kill it. It is the synthesis section of the product feedback loop — the packet that connects market evidence to a scoped build decision.

launch-readiness.reveal: No falsifiable test and no metric. 'They all want it' is stated preference, and stated preference is the cheapest thing a customer gives away. Launch readiness demands a revealed-behavior experiment ('40% of a 200-user cohort complete the new activation step in week one') plus the number below which you kill it. Without a pre-set threshold, you will rationalize any result as success — the enthusiasm becomes the evidence, which is exactly the trap.

# Launch Readiness — Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## 1. Segment & discovery evidence
- Segment: solo operators onboarding <30 days
- Pain (from 9 interviews): manual data import stalls 6 of 9 before first value
- Quote: "I gave up importing and just never came back"

## 2. Experiment (must be able to return NO)
- Type: concierge test — we import for 40 new signups by hand
- Reveals behavior, not opinion: do imported users activate?

## 3. Metric tree
- North star: 30-day retention
  - Activation metric (leading): % reaching 'first value' in 48h
  - Instrumented event: import_completed -> first_dashboard_view

## 4. Invalidation threshold (committed BEFORE results)
- KILL if: activation < 35% in the concierge cohort
- PIVOT if: activation high BUT week-1 retention < baseline

## 5. Decision memo
- Chosen: build automated import ONLY if concierge clears 35%
- Rejected: build the importer now on interview enthusiasm alone
- Reversal condition: retention un-lifted at day 30 -> roll back
- Reviewer objection: "is 35% just the number that lets you ship?"

Segment + discovery evidence: Name the market segment and the pain in the customer's words. 'Everyone' is not a segment; a quote from a real interview beats a paragraph of your own summary.

A falsifiable experiment: A concierge test measures revealed behavior — do hand-imported users actually activate? The invariant: it must be able to return 'no'. A test that can only say 'yes' is theater.
The metric tree: Separate the north star (retention) from the leading activation metric, and name the exact instrumented event. If you can't name the event, you can't measure the result.
The invalidation threshold — committed first: 35% is written BEFORE the data. This is the line the whole gate turns on. Set it after and you will move it to whatever the result was.

Chosen vs rejected + reversal: The rejected option is 'build on enthusiasm now'. Naming the reversal condition (retention un-lifted at day 30) makes the decision honest, not a one-way rationalization.
The reviewer objection, in writing: Pre-answer the sharpest challenge — 'is 35% just the ship number?' — by showing it came from the 6-of-9 stall rate, not from convenience.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

# Writing the packet, one section at a time
#
# Mission: Take one product idea you are about to build and write the Launch Readiness packet: the customer evidence you have, the ONE experiment that could invalidate the idea, the activation metric it must move, and the invalidation threshold that would make you kill or pivot it — before a line of the real feature ships.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only readiness_gate at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Read your experiment aloud. Can it return 'no' and kill the idea? If every outcome confirms the build, it is theater — redesign it to measure revealed behavior, not stated preference.
# 2. Point to ONE activation metric with a named instrumented event. If you have three vague metrics or none you can log, you cannot prove the result.
# 3. Confirm the invalidation threshold is a number written BEFORE any data exists. If you set it after peeking, it validated nothing.
# 4. Check the decision memo names a rejected approach and a reversal condition — not just the option you already favored.
# 5. Hand the packet to a peer: can they state what you would do just above and just below the threshold, without you narrating? If not, the threshold is ambiguous.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

ITEMS = [
    ("discovery-evidence", True, True, 3),
    ("launch-experiment-designed", True, True, 3),
    ("activation-metric-instrumented", True, False, 3),
    ("invalidation-threshold-registered", True, True, 3),
    ("rollback-flag-tested", True, True, 2),
    ("support-macros-drafted", False, False, 1),
    ("pricing-impact-reviewed", False, True, 1),
]
BAR = 80.0


def readiness_gate(items, bar_pct):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

score, blockers, verdict = readiness_gate(ITEMS, BAR)
print(f"weighted readiness: {score:.0f}%")
for b in blockers:
    print(f"BLOCKER: {b}")
print(f"verdict: {verdict}")
repaired = [(n, r, True if n == "activation-metric-instrumented" else d, w)
            for n, r, d, w in ITEMS]
score2, blockers2, verdict2 = readiness_gate(repaired, BAR)
print(f"after 2-day repair: {score2:.0f}%, blockers: {len(blockers2)} -> {verdict2}")
launch-readiness.check:
weighted readiness: 75%
BLOCKER: activation-metric-instrumented
verdict: NO-GO
after 2-day repair: 94%, blockers: 0 -> GO

storyboard.say: Everything starts with customer discovery — the raw market evidence that some people seem excited about the idea.
Discovery isn't proof. It designs one falsifiable experiment — a bet sharp enough that a real result could kill it.
The experiment measures a single activation metric — the concrete number the feature must actually move.
Now the gate: that metric is compared against an invalidation threshold committed BEFORE you looked at the result.
At or above the threshold, and only then, do you earn a scoped build — real engineering behind a proven bet.
Below the threshold, you kill or pivot. The pre-committed number is what gives you permission to stop.
This dashed path is the failure the gate exists to block: shipping straight from a hunch, skipping the experiment entirely.
The invariant: write the killing number down before the result arrives — otherwise nine weeks ship to silence.

post-launch-analysis.text: The feature shipped Tuesday. By Friday the launch channel is full of screenshots — 'usage is up!' — and the PM wants to double down. One engineer pulls the retention curve, sees D7 already collapsing to a flat line of nobody, and asks the question that stops the celebration: 'Did anyone come back?'

Post launch analysis is the last move in the product feedback loop: it turns raw launch telemetry into a keep/kill/iterate decision that a team can defend. This is Section 5 of the packet you carry through the course — where market evidence finally connects to a scoped engineering decision.

post-launch-analysis.prompt: A launch dashboard shows daily active users jumped 40% in week one. Before you call it a win — what is wrong with using that as your success signal? Answer before reading on.
post-launch-analysis.reveal: It measures curiosity, not value. A launch spike is activation — people trying the thing once because it is new and you announced it. Whether the feature works is a RETENTION question: did those users come back on day 7, day 30? A 40% activation bump with a retention curve that flatlines is a feature nobody needed, dressed as a hit. Post launch analysis reads the second curve, not the first.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Context
- Feature launched: one-tap checkout, to 20% of buyers on 2026-06-08
- Hypothesis: friction, not intent, was killing conversion

## Metric tree (pre-declared)
- Activation: % of exposed buyers who tap the new button    (leading)
- Retention: % who return + reuse it within 7 days          (the real signal)
- North star: repeat-purchase rate for the cohort

## Invalidation threshold (dated 2026-06-07, BEFORE launch)
- KILL if 7-day reuse < 15% OR repeat-purchase not up vs control

## Observed (7 days post-launch)
- Activation: 41% tapped it (well above expectation)
- Retention: 9% reused within 7 days  <-- below the 15% kill line

# Writing the Decision Packet, one line at a time
#
# Mission: Take one feature you shipped (or a realistic one) and run its post-launch analysis into a decision: read the launch metrics against a pre-declared invalidation threshold, then write the Decision Packet that says keep, kill, or iterate — and why the numbers force that call.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only cohort_read at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Your invalidation threshold has a date EARLIER than your observed data. If not, you set the bar after seeing the result — re-do it against a genuinely pre-committed number.
# 2. You report retention (D7/D30 reuse), not only activation. A packet with only a launch-spike metric is measuring curiosity, not value.
# 3. The chosen decision (keep/kill/iterate) follows mechanically from comparing observed metrics to the threshold — a reviewer with your numbers reaches the same call.
# 4. You named the rejected option and why the evidence rules it out. If nothing was rejected, you did not face the tempting wrong decision.
# 5. There is a reversal condition on any 'iterate', so it cannot become a permanent excuse to keep a feature that failed its bar.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

EXPOSED = 400
ACTIVATED = 128
RETAINED = 44
ACTIVATION_BAR = 30.0
RETENTION_BAR = 15.0


def cohort_read(activated, retained, exposed):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

act, ret = cohort_read(ACTIVATED, RETAINED, EXPOSED)
act_pass = act >= ACTIVATION_BAR
ret_pass = ret >= RETENTION_BAR
print(f"activation: {ACTIVATED}/{EXPOSED} = {act:.1f}% (bar {ACTIVATION_BAR:.0f}%) {'PASS' if act_pass else 'FAIL'}")
print(f"retention: {RETAINED}/{EXPOSED} = {ret:.1f}% (bar {RETENTION_BAR:.0f}%) {'PASS' if ret_pass else 'FAIL'}")
passes = int(act_pass) + int(ret_pass)
verdict = "KEEP & widen" if passes == 2 else ("ITERATE" if passes == 1 else "KILL")
print(f"decision map verdict: {verdict}")
if passes == 1:
    failing = "retention" if not ret_pass else "activation"
    print(f"iteration scope: diagnose the {failing} leg before touching anything else")

post-launch-analysis.subtitle: Launch telemetry splits into activation and retention; each is compared to the pre-declared threshold. The failure path (metrics below bar) and the repair path (iterate + re-test) are both drawn — the boundary case is the whole skill.

storyboard.say: It starts with launch telemetry — raw usage flowing in after the feature ships, muted until we split it into the two signals that matter.
We measure two things from that stream: activation, whether people used it, and retention, whether they came back.
Both signals get compared against the same gate — the invalidation threshold you wrote down and dated before any data existed.
When activation and retention both clear the bar, the decision is easy: keep the feature and scale it.
This is the trap — activation is up but retention is collapsing. Weak retention isn't a win, it routes to the repair path: iterate and re-test.
If the metrics fall below the pre-declared bar outright, you take the failure path — kill it or roll back, no re-litigating the threshold.
The repair path loops back: ship the change and re-observe fresh telemetry against the same untouched threshold.
The invariant holds the whole tree together — the threshold is dated before the data. A bar moved to fit the result is not analysis.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Context
- Feature launched: one-tap checkout, to 20% of buyers on 2026-06-08
- Hypothesis: friction, not intent, was killing conversion

## Metric tree (pre-declared)
- Activation: % of exposed buyers who tap the new button    (leading)
- Retention: % who return + reuse it within 7 days          (the real signal)
- North star: repeat-purchase rate for the cohort

## Invalidation threshold (dated 2026-06-07, BEFORE launch)
- KILL if 7-day reuse < 15% OR repeat-purchase not up vs control

## Observed (7 days post-launch)
- Activation: 41% tapped it (well above expectation)
- Retention: 9% reused within 7 days  <-- below the 15% kill line
- Repeat-purchase: flat vs control (no lift)

## Decision
- Chosen: ITERATE — activation proves discoverability; retention says the flow still leaks
- Rejected: KEEP/scale — the reuse curve is below the pre-set kill bar
- Reversal condition: if reuse stays < 15% after the address-autofill fix, KILL

iteration-loop.text: Two founders ship the same feature. One watches signups tick up and calls it traction; the other pre-committed that under 20% week-2 retention means the idea is wrong — and at 11%, kills it Monday. Six months later one is still 'iterating' on a corpse and the other is on their third, better bet.

The Iteration Loop is the engine that turns market evidence into build decisions: assumption → experiment → metric → decision → repeat. It sits at the synthesis of everything before it — discovery, PRD, MVP scope, metric trees, instrumentation — and produces the one artifact a reviewer can actually audit: a decision packet, not a note.

iteration-loop.prompt: You launch an experiment and activation looks 'pretty good.' Before you decide to keep building — what is wrong with judging 'pretty good' now? Answer before reading on.
iteration-loop.reveal: 'Pretty good' is a threshold you invented after seeing the number, which means the number can never surprise you — you will always find a way to call it a win. The loop's whole value is a pre-committed invalidation threshold: 'below 20% week-2 retention, the assumption is dead.' Set after the data, every result confirms the idea; set before, the experiment can actually kill a bad bet and save you a quarter.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Context
- Idea: charge $49 for a guided onboarding call on top of self-serve signup
- Market segment: solo founders on the free plan, week 1

## Riskiest assumption
- "Free-plan founders will PAY to be onboarded, not just accept it free."
- If false: the whole paid-onboarding line has no willingness-to-pay; kill it.

## Experiment (smallest that can invalidate)
- Fake-door: add a $49 "Book onboarding call" button; on click, capture card intent
- Ships in 1 day; 200 free-plan users see it; no call is actually delivered yet

## Activation metric + invalidation threshold (set BEFORE data)
- Metric: paid-intent rate = card-entered / button-shown
- Persevere >= 6%   Pivot 2-6% (price/offer wrong, demand real)   Kill < 2%

## Result & decision
- Observed: 1.5% (3 of 200) entered card intent
- Decision: KILL paid onboarding; the willingness-to-pay assumption is invalidated

## Rejected approach
- Rejected: run a 4-week retention cohort first (slow, expensive, tests the wrong risk)

## Expected failure / reviewer objection / repair / capstone
- (see steps below)

Metric + threshold BEFORE data: One activation metric, three pre-committed bands. This line is the whole lesson — written before you look, so the number can surprise you.
Result → decision: 1.5% falls in the kill band you set in advance. The decision is forced by the threshold, not negotiated after. This is a real kill, not a story.
The rejected approach: A slow retention cohort tests the wrong risk first. Cheapest test of the riskiest assumption wins — same discipline as a diagnostic route.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

KILL_BAR = 32.0
DEADLINE_TURN = 5

    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

deltas, slope, projection = trend_read(TURNS, DEADLINE_TURN)

storyboard.say: Every loop starts here: name the one assumption that, if false, sinks the whole idea. Not the safe one — the riskiest one.
From that assumption you design the smallest experiment whose result could actually prove it wrong — nothing bigger.
The experiment emits one activation metric — a single number, like week-two retention, not a dashboard of vanity charts.
Here is the fork that decides everything: you compare that number against a kill-threshold you committed to before any data arrived.
This dashed path is the failure mode: skip the threshold, read the metric as a story, and talk yourself into traction that isn't there.
Honor the threshold instead: if the number falls below it, the decision memo says pivot or kill — on the rule, not the hope.
A killed bet isn't a dead end; the memo feeds the next riskiest assumption, and the loop turns again toward a better idea.

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## Context
- Idea: charge $49 for a guided onboarding call on top of self-serve signup
- Market segment: solo founders on the free plan, week 1

## Riskiest assumption
- "Free-plan founders will PAY to be onboarded, not just accept it free."
- If false: the whole paid-onboarding line has no willingness-to-pay; kill it.

## Experiment (smallest that can invalidate)
- Fake-door: add a $49 "Book onboarding call" button; on click, capture card intent
- Ships in 1 day; 200 free-plan users see it; no call is actually delivered yet

## Activation metric + invalidation threshold (set BEFORE data)
- Metric: paid-intent rate = card-entered / button-shown
- Persevere >= 6%   Pivot 2-6% (price/offer wrong, demand real)   Kill < 2%

## Result & decision
- Observed: 1.5% (3 of 200) entered card intent
- Decision: KILL paid onboarding; the willingness-to-pay assumption is invalidated

## Rejected approach
- Rejected: run a 4-week retention cohort first (slow, expensive, tests the wrong risk)

## Expected failure / reviewer objection / repair / capstone
- (see steps below)

# Decision: Kill freemium, ship 14-day trial
> BLUF: Activation is 3.1x higher on trial (41% vs 13%). Recommend cutting freemium next sprint.

## Evidence
- Discovery: 9/12 interviews said free tier felt 'crippled', not 'free'
- Experiment: A/B, n=1,840, 14 days, activation = created-first-project
- Result: trial 41% activation vs freemium 13% (p<0.01)

## Selected approach: 14-day trial
## Rejected approach: freemium — cheaper CAC, but activation too low to retain

## Reversal condition (invalidation threshold)
- If trial activation drops below 25% at 30-day cohort, revert to freemium

## Reviewer objection + repair
- 'Trial hurts top-of-funnel.' Signups fell 12%, but activated users rose 2.6x.
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.
BLUF — the decision first: The stakeholder reads one line and knows the call and the number behind it. Never make them scroll to find whether you're recommending anything.
Evidence, in loop order: Discovery framed it, the experiment tested it, the metric decided it. Sample size and p-value signal this is measurement, not anecdote.
Selected vs rejected: Naming the rejected option — and its real upside — proves you weighed the tradeoff, not just championed a favorite.
The invalidation threshold: The trust-maker: the exact metric value that reverses the decision. A stakeholder can own a call that carries its own kill-switch.
Objection + repair: Pre-answer the sharpest counter. 'Signups fell but activated users rose 2.6x' turns the obvious objection into supporting evidence.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

stakeholder-communication.text: The senior tell is the reversal condition, not the confidence. Anyone can present a decision they believe; naming the exact metric value that would prove you wrong — 'revert if 30-day activation drops below 25%' — is what makes a stakeholder trust a call they did not run. NIST AI RMF calls for mechanisms to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems whose performance is inconsistent with intended use (MANAGE 2.4), and DORA emphasizes measurable rollback/recovery — together supporting the practice of defining conditions under which a decision is reversed. (NIST does not use the term "reversal threshold" and does not call it "the mark of a governed decision.")

# Customer Experiment & Metric Decision Packet

## 1. Context (from discovery)
- Segment: solo operators onboarding in <10 min; 8 interviews
- Pain (their words): "I signed up, hit the blank dashboard, and left"
- Assumption under test: a guided first-run raises activation

## 2. Metric tree
- North star: week-2 retention
  - driver: activation (reached first 'aha' <10 min)  <-- the lever
  - guardrail: day-7 retention must not drop

## 3. Experiment
- Change: guided first-run vs blank dashboard (50/50, instrumented)
- Primary metric: activation rate
- INVALIDATION THRESHOLD (pre-registered): ship ONLY if
  activation >= 28% AND day-7 retention stays >= 40%
- Sample / stop rule: 600 signups per arm, or 14 days

## 4. Decision memo
- Chosen: ship guided first-run (activation 31%, retention 41%)
- Rejected: full onboarding redesign -- 3-sprint cost, not scoped to the driver
- Reversal condition: roll back if 30-day retention regresses vs control

## 5. Reviewer objection + repair
- Objection: "31% could be novelty, not activation"
- Repair: hold-out cohort re-measured at day 30 before full rollout

## 6. Capstone connection
- Reuses: discovery notes, metric tree, experiment, decision memo, feedback hook
steps: Write the expected metric or classification before executing the reference.

Section 1 — ground it in discovery: Quote the pain in the customer's words, not yours. The assumption under test must be one sentence and falsifiable — 'a guided first-run raises activation', not 'improve onboarding'.

Section 2 — the metric tree picks ONE lever: North star → driver → guardrail. Activation is the driver you can move; the guardrail (day-7 retention) stops you from winning the metric while losing the product.

Section 3 — the invalidation threshold: This is the line that separates the packet from a note. Written BEFORE the run, with an AND clause so you cannot cherry-pick one metric. The stop rule keeps the experiment from running until it flatters you.

Section 4 — the decision memo names the rejected option: Chosen, rejected (with WHY — the redesign wasn't scoped to the driver), and a reversal condition. A decision with no rejected option is a preference, not a memo.
Section 5 — pre-empt the reviewer: Name the strongest objection to your own result ('novelty, not activation') and attach the repair. This is what turns 78 into a defensible pass.
Section 6 — the capstone connection: The packet is portfolio evidence only if the next bet can reuse it unchanged in structure. Name what carries forward.
Change one input across the registered threshold and explain why the decision reverses.

# Writing the packet, section by section
#
# Mission: Take one real product bet you are facing and assemble the whole course into a single reviewable artifact: a customer_experiment_and_metric_decision_packet.md that runs the loop end-to-end — discovery evidence, the framed problem, the metric tree, the experiment with an invalidation threshold, the decision memo, and the launch/feedback hook.
# Novice workflow:
# 1. Predict the decision before running the code.
# 2. Trace the supplied fixtures and name the weakest assumption.
# 3. Implement only run_chain at the TODO.
# 4. Match every output line, add one boundary case, and retain it as a regression.
#
# Evidence checklist:
# 1. Section 1 quotes real discovery pain in the customer's words, and states one falsifiable assumption under test.
# 2. The metric tree names a north star, ONE driver you can move, and a guardrail — not a single orphan metric.
# 3. The invalidation threshold was written BEFORE the experiment ran and has an AND clause, so no single metric can be cherry-picked.
# 4. A stop rule (sample size or time box) exists, so the run cannot continue until the data flatters you.
# 5. The decision memo names the chosen option, the rejected option WITH a reason, and a reversal condition.
# 6. You pre-empted the strongest objection to your own result and attached a concrete repair — and the packet is reusable, unchanged in structure, on the next bet.
#
# Local execution is practice feedback only; it cannot create mastery evidence.

DISCOVERY_UNPROMPTED = (9, 7)
DISCOVERY_WORKAROUND = (6, 5)
EXPERIMENT = (124, 400, 28.0)
RETENTION = (48, 124, 15.0)

GATES = [
    ("discovery", None, None, True),
    ("experiment", EXPERIMENT[0] / EXPERIMENT[1] * 100, EXPERIMENT[2], True),
    ("retention", RETENTION[0] / RETENTION[1] * 100, RETENTION[2], True),
]


def run_chain(gates):
    # TODO: implement the evidence calculation from the supplied product fixtures.
    # Return data, not a persuasive verdict; the caller owns the explicit decision threshold.
    raise NotImplementedError("complete the product evidence decision")

results = run_chain(GATES)
for name, ok in results:
    if name == "discovery":
        print(f"gate 1 discovery: {DISCOVERY_UNPROMPTED[0]}/12 unprompted (>= {DISCOVERY_UNPROMPTED[1]}), {DISCOVERY_WORKAROUND[0]}/12 workaround (>= {DISCOVERY_WORKAROUND[1]}) -> {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}")
    elif name == "experiment":
        print(f"gate 2 experiment: {EXPERIMENT[0]}/{EXPERIMENT[1]} = {EXPERIMENT[0] / EXPERIMENT[1] * 100:.1f}% (bar {EXPERIMENT[2]:.0f}%) -> {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}")
    else:
        print(f"gate 3 retention: {RETENTION[0]}/{RETENTION[1]} = {RETENTION[0] / RETENTION[1] * 100:.1f}% (bar {RETENTION[2]:.0f}%) -> {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}")
passes = sum(1 for _, ok in results if ok)
failed = [n for n, ok in results if not ok]
if passes == 3:
    verdict = "SHIP wide"
elif passes == 2 and failed == ["retention"]:
    verdict = "ITERATE - do not scale a leaky bucket"
else:
    verdict = "KILL"
print(f"chain verdict (day-1 map): {verdict}")
print("ship scope: roll out wide behind the day-1 reversal rule -> re-measure the day-30 hold-out before removing the guardrail")

storyboard.say: Evidence enters here: three interview quotes and a shaky activation number. Customer discovery grounds the problem frame instead of a founder's hunch.
The problem frame picks one driver from the metric tree, so we chase a single number, not a vibe.
The metric tree defines the success metric the experiment must move, converting the driver into a testable target.
Before running, the invalidation threshold sets the kill line — the bet must be killable by evidence you defined first.
Clear the threshold and the experiment produces a decision memo naming the option you rejected — a packet a skeptic would sign.
Miss the threshold and it routes back to the problem frame to repair — the loop refuses to ship on a vibe.
The scoped decision becomes a scoped build; launch and feedback flow back into discovery so the next bet inherits a proven loop.
Pricing stays deliberately outside this packet — noted, but not wired into the decision this loop is closing.

product-capstone.intro: Prove the packet holds — no vibes:
items: Section 1 quotes real discovery pain in the customer's words, and states one falsifiable assumption under test.
The metric tree names a north star, ONE driver you can move, and a guardrail — not a single orphan metric.
The invalidation threshold was written BEFORE the experiment ran and has an AND clause, so no single metric can be cherry-picked.
A stop rule (sample size or time box) exists, so the run cannot continue until the data flatters you.
The decision memo names the chosen option, the rejected option WITH a reason, and a reversal condition.
You pre-empted the strongest objection to your own result and attached a concrete repair — and the packet is reusable, unchanged in structure, on the next bet.

prompts: Roll-call the loop: name each course lesson (discovery, frame, metric tree, experiment, decision, launch, feedback) and the exact section of your packet where it lives.
Explain why the invalidation threshold — not the result — is the line between a real experiment and a demo, using your own packet's numbers.
Which option did you reject, and why was it not scoped to the driver in your metric tree? Defend the rejection as a judgment, not an oversight.

product-capstone.excellent: Passing evidence plus a decision-reversing fixture, retained regression, rejected option, reviewer objection, and transfer: You came in able to argue for a feature in a room and you leave able to do the thing that actually decides the outcome: turn customer evidence into one scoped, falsifiable, reviewable bet — with a kill line you wrote before you looked. Now change the context and watch the invariant hold: a different market segment, a pricing-model change instead of an activation lever, a retention bet instead of a conversion one. The metric moves, the sample size moves, the threshold moves — but the loop does not. You do not just talk about product judgment now. You can run the loop.
